original_complete_jsonld.name: Self-Employed Mortgage Guidance
original_complete_jsonld.description: Compare self-employed mortgage options in Austin and across Texas. See how tax returns, bank statements, 1099s, P&L and eligible assets can support qualification.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a special mortgage because I’m self-employed?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Conventional, FHA, VA and jumbo options may be available when your income, credit, funds and property meet the program’s requirements. An alternative-documentation mortgage is worth comparing when a different supported income calculation addresses a specific obstacle.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to change my tax deductions before buying a home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with an accurate mortgage-income review of your existing records. Some deductions receive permitted adjustments, and another documentation method may fit. Discuss tax-planning decisions with your tax professional; a mortgage review should not assume that giving up legitimate deductions is your only option.

mainEntity.name: Can I qualify with less than two years of self-employment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some programs allow shorter histories under specific conditions. Business age, your prior related work, documented earnings and the business’s ability to continue all matter. A 12-month bank-statement option does not automatically mean 12 months in business is enough.

mainEntity.name: Can I use business funds for the down payment or closing costs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Possibly. The lender must establish that you can access the funds and may need to evaluate how withdrawing them affects the business. Tell Adam early if the same business will provide both your qualifying income and your money for closing.

mainEntity.name: Can K-1 income help me qualify?

acceptedAnswer.text: Potentially. A K-1 reports income from an entity; it is not a separate loan type or automatic proof of cash available to you. Ownership, distributions, business strength and access to income determine the analysis. See how K-1 income is reviewed.

mainEntity.name: What credit score and down payment do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the path. On bank statement loans, minimum credit starts at 620 to 660 and the strongest files buy with 10% down (90% loan-to-value). Conventional, FHA and VA follow their own published minimums when your tax returns support the loan.

mainEntity.name: Can self-employed borrowers get a mortgage in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Self-employed borrowers can qualify for conventional, FHA, VA, jumbo or eligible alternative-documentation mortgages. The right path depends on documented income, credit, funds and the property, rather than employment status alone.

mainEntity.name: What is a bank statement loan and how does it work?

acceptedAnswer.text: It qualifies you on 12 or 24 months of deposits instead of tax-return income. Business deposits are reduced by an expense factor, 50% by default or as low as 10% to 15% with a qualified expense letter from your tax preparer. Transfers, loan proceeds and refunds are excluded first.

mainEntity.name: What do I need to qualify for a self-employed mortgage in Austin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with your property goal, business type, ownership, time in business and how you earn income. The lender then verifies the accepted income method, credit, debts, down payment or equity and reserves. Tax returns, statements, 1099s or a P&L may be needed depending on the program.

mainEntity.name: Why do write-offs affect my mortgage qualification?

acceptedAnswer.text: Deductions can reduce reported business profit, but mortgage income is not always the bottom-line tax figure. Conventional rules permit certain adjustments, and another supported documentation method may fit. Compare both calculations before assuming deductions prevent qualification.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between a bank statement loan, 1099 loan, and P&L loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three ways to document the same business. A bank statement loan averages 12 or 24 months of deposits minus an expense factor. A 1099 loan starts from gross 1099 income with a flat 10% expense factor. A P&L loan uses a CPA-prepared profit-and-loss statement. I run all three, because the one that qualifies you for the most is rarely the one with the best rate.

mainEntity.name: Can a self-employed business owner in Austin get a mortgage without tax returns?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Bank statement, 1099, P&L and asset-depletion programs qualify you without tax-return income. Bank statement loans use 12 or 24 months of deposits with a 50% default expense factor; 1099 loans use gross 1099 income minus 10%.

mainEntity.name: Why do tax returns make me look poorer than I am as a business owner?

acceptedAnswer.text: Taxable income and mortgage qualifying income can differ. A conventional review considers permitted adjustments, such as eligible add-backs, along with income history and business performance. An alternative method may use eligible deposits, a P&L, 1099 earnings, or assets. Compare the supported calculations before assuming the tax return rules out a suitable loan.

mainEntity.name: What is the 2026 conforming loan limit in Travis County?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2026 baseline conforming loan limit for a one-unit property in Travis County is $832,750, up $26,250 from 2025. No Texas county qualifies as high-cost in 2026, so the same one-unit limit applies statewide. A loan above the applicable conforming limit is a jumbo loan; whether it is a qualified mortgage or Non-QM is a separate classification. Source: FHFA 2026 Conforming Loan Limit Values.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between bank statement, P&L, and 1099 loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three ways to document the same business. Bank statement loans average 12 or 24 months of deposits minus an expense factor (50% by default). 1099 loans start from gross 1099 income with a flat 10% factor. P&L loans use a CPA-prepared profit-and-loss statement, with 700-plus credit and up to 80% loan-to-value.

mainEntity.name: How does asset depletion work for high-net-worth Austin borrowers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Asset-depletion programs calculate qualifying income from eligible documented assets after required deductions. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac publish specific agency methods; non-QM asset eligibility, discounts, divisors, leverage, reserves, and documentation vary by investor and current program.

mainEntity.name: What is a DSCR loan and when does it beat a self-employed program?

acceptedAnswer.text: A DSCR loan is generally a business-purpose investment-property mortgage that primarily evaluates qualifying rent relative to PITIA. Personal-income, credit, asset, reserve, guaranty, entity, rent, and property-document requirements vary by investor and program. Primary- and second-home borrowers need a different eligible loan type.

mainEntity.name: Can K-1 income from a partnership or S-corp qualify for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: K-1 and entity income may qualify after a current analysis of ownership, distributions, business liquidity, income history, and required tax documents. The applicable agency or investor guide determines how income, losses, and eligible adjustments are treated.

mainEntity.name: What loan programs cover one-time-close custom construction in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: A one-time-close structure combines construction and permanent financing at the initial closing. A two-time-close structure uses separate construction and permanent loans. Eligibility, loan size, builder, budget, payment, rate-lock, draw, completion, conversion, title, closing-cost, and legal requirements vary by lender, program, property, and transaction.

mainEntity.name: Will the rate be higher than a conventional loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Pricing varies by date, program, credit, leverage, property, documentation, lock period, and other scenario details. Compare same-day written quotes or Loan Estimates using matching assumptions. A future refinance may be possible, but it is not guaranteed.

mainEntity.name: How fast does a self-employed mortgage typically close in Austin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pre-approval usually takes one business day once your file is complete. P&L and jumbo files typically close in 25 to 35 days when documents, appraisal and title are clean.

mainEntity.name: Can my LLC or S-corp own the property?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a rental, yes: DSCR loans allow LLC ownership. For a home you live in, title usually goes in your personal name or an eligible revocable trust. Ask your attorney and CPA about liability and tax effects before moving title.

mainEntity.name: How much down payment do business owners need?

acceptedAnswer.text: From 10% on a primary residence with bank statement or 1099 programs on the strongest files, and 20% on P&L-only programs (80% maximum loan-to-value). Conventional loans follow their own published minimums when your tax returns support the loan.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to pay myself a bigger salary from my S-corp to qualify?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with a review of your existing compensation and business records before changing salary. Depending on the rules and ownership, a lender may consider wages and other eligible business income, with adjustments for access, distributions, business strength, and history. A higher paycheck alone does not establish more qualifying income. Coordinate any compensation change with your tax professional.

mainEntity.name: Can I use money from my business account for the down payment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, yes. Lenders accept business funds when you own the business and the withdrawal won’t hurt it, typically shown with a CPA letter or a review of business cash flow. Tell me early if the same business provides both your income and your down payment.

mainEntity.name: How far ahead of buying should I talk to a lender if I'm self-employed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start when the purchase becomes a realistic goal, especially before major business, compensation, or financing changes. An early review can identify records or history that still need to be established. If you are already looking at homes, share your timing now; the review will determine what can proceed and what needs more preparation.

mainEntity.name: What should I ask my CPA before I apply?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask which records explain current business earnings, whether planned entity or tax changes affect those records, and what preparation or verification the CPA can provide if requested. The mortgage professional should calculate qualifying income under the selected program; your CPA advises on taxes. With your permission, coordinating those questions can help avoid missing documentation.

mainEntity.name: I own several businesses. Which ones does the lender look at?

acceptedAnswer.text: Provide a clear map of your entities, ownership, income, losses, and guarantees. The lender reviews businesses used for qualifying income and may need to consider other business losses or obligations even when their income is not being used. The program determines the treatment. Begin with a summary, then provide required returns and K-1s through secure collection.

mainEntity.name: My income dropped last year, or it's seasonal. Am I stuck?

acceptedAnswer.text: A decline or seasonal pattern needs explanation, not an automatic conclusion. The lender will review current earnings, the reason for the change, and whether the income appears stable under the selected program. A longer average can help explain seasonality but does not cancel an ongoing decline, and a shorter statement period does not guarantee eligibility.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to give up my tax write-offs to buy a house?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Begin with an accurate review of your existing returns and any permitted adjustments. Another documentation method may fit, but it still must support the loan under its own rules. Discuss deductions, amendments, and other tax decisions with your tax professional rather than changing them solely to pursue a mortgage calculation.

mainEntity.name: What is a bank statement loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bank statement loan is a mortgage option that uses eligible personal or business deposits as the primary evidence for a self-employed income calculation. The lender reviews deposit sources, expenses, ownership and income trends alongside credit, debts, funds and the property.

mainEntity.name: Does every deposit count as income?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The review separates eligible income from transfers, borrowed funds, refunds, and deposits without a documented business source. Program examples include a 50% business expense factor, a supported lower factor, or a 15% to 85% schedule based on business type and headcount. Some programs require a written explanation when a deposit exceeds a month’s qualifying income. The selected program controls the calculation and documentation.

mainEntity.name: Will I still need tax returns or other records?

acceptedAnswer.text: A selected bank-statement program may use eligible deposits as the primary income documentation. That does not guarantee a file will need no tax returns, transcripts or other records. Business verification, deposit explanations and additional documents can still be required for the specific file.

mainEntity.name: Can I use personal statements instead of business statements?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some programs accept personal statements. One program method counts eligible business-to-personal transfers at 100% with no additional expense reduction, supported by two or three months of business statements. In these examples, mixed accounts receive business-account expense treatment; ownership requirements include 25% for a personal-statement method and 50% for a business-statement method. Confirm the current method and ownership requirement; the same earnings cannot be counted twice.

mainEntity.name: Does a 12-month program mean I only need one year in business?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Statement period and business history are separate requirements. These program examples require two years of self-employment; one calls for an additional 12 months of statements if the first 12 do not establish stability. Confirm the selected lender’s current history requirement.

mainEntity.name: Can a bank statement loan be used to buy or refinance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Programs may allow purchases or refinances. These program examples include purchases up to 90% loan-to-value, cash-out examples up to 80%, and loan limits of $3 million to $4 million. Availability and combinations of these limits depend on current program requirements and the full file. For a rental property, also compare DSCR financing based on the property’s rental income.

mainEntity.name: Will it cost more than a conventional mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: It may. Different documentation can carry different pricing and down-payment requirements. If your tax returns support conventional financing, compare it with the bank-statement option. I compare available offers using the same assumptions and pricing date, including rate, points, fees, payment, and cash required.

mainEntity.name: I'm a 1099 contractor. Can I qualify on my deposits?

acceptedAnswer.text: Depending on your file, we can compare 12 or 24 months of eligible deposits with a 1099-only program where available. One 1099 program example uses gross 1099 income with a 10% expense factor. Compare the actual eligibility, expense treatment, and supported income under each method; additional deposits are not automatically qualifying income.

mainEntity.name: What if I co-mingle business and personal accounts?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mixed accounts do not automatically rule out a review. In these program examples, a mixed personal/business account receives business-account treatment, with the selected expense factor applied to eligible deposits; one standard factor is 50%. Confirm the lender’s method for your accounts. Separate accounts can make the source and movement of money easier to document. The same earnings cannot be counted twice; personal-account treatment still depends on the selected program.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between 12 and 24 month programs?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 12-month review uses a more recent year; 24 months can show two business cycles and seasonal patterns. The lender evaluates trends and sustainability. Neither period is automatically better, and the statement period is separate from the required time in business.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: These program examples have minimum credit scores of 620 to 660 at reduced leverage. The selected program may require a higher score for the loan amount, loan-to-value, or property. Stronger credit may improve available terms, but it does not establish eligibility by itself.

mainEntity.name: How much down payment?

acceptedAnswer.text: These program examples allow primary-residence purchases with as little as 10% down (90% loan-to-value) and cash-out refinances up to 80% loan-to-value. Lower credit, larger loans, property details, and other program conditions may require more equity. Confirm the current requirement for your file.

mainEntity.name: How long does closing take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Timing depends on the income review, the complete file, appraisal, and title. I identify the expected documents early, and Tiffany coordinates questions and updates. We can discuss a realistic timeline once we know the file; a one-day pre-approval should not be assumed.

mainEntity.name: What is a P&L only mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A P&L only mortgage is a Non-QM home loan that qualifies self-employed borrowers on a CPA-prepared profit and loss statement instead of tax returns. The lender uses the net income on the P&L (plus standard add-backs like depreciation) as monthly qualifying income. Most programs require the P&L cover at least 12 months and include current year-to-date results.

mainEntity.name: Who can prepare the P&L?

acceptedAnswer.text: A licensed CPA, an IRS enrolled agent, or a CTEC-registered tax preparer, and that person must have prepared or reviewed your most recent business tax return. The preparer signs the statement on letterhead with their license or PTIN number, and you sign it too.

mainEntity.name: How is qualifying income calculated from a P&L?

acceptedAnswer.text: The underwriter takes the P&L net income, adds back non-cash deductions (depreciation, amortization), and divides by the months in the P&L period. A 24-month P&L showing $480,000 net income plus $24,000 depreciation add-back equals $504,000 ÷ 24 = $21,000/month qualifying income. Ownership percentage is applied if the borrower doesn't own 100%.

mainEntity.name: How is a P&L loan different from a bank statement loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bank statement loans use deposits with a generic expense factor (often 50%) — accurate if your real expenses match the default, off if they don't. P&L only uses your CPA's actual numbers, so a service business with 20% real expenses qualifies for more than the 50% bank statement default would allow. Higher-expense businesses sometimes qualify for more on bank statement. The P&L route prices the file to reality.

mainEntity.name: What's a hybrid P&L program?

acceptedAnswer.text: A hybrid pairs the P&L with two or three months of business bank statements, and the deposits have to corroborate the revenue. One program requires eligible deposits of at least 80% of the P&L’s gross monthly revenue; another requires revenue and deposits within 10% of each other. If deposits fall short, the lender qualifies you on the deposits. The hybrid is what opens leverage above the P&L-only caps.

mainEntity.name: What if my CPA refuses to prepare the P&L?

acceptedAnswer.text: It happens. Some CPAs decline due to AICPA professional standards around compilation engagements and liability. If your CPA won't do it, an IRS Enrolled Agent (EA) or CTEC-registered tax preparer is the standard fallback. Most lender programs accept EA-prepared P&Ls as equivalent to CPA-prepared. We have CPAs and EAs in network who'll handle this.

mainEntity.name: Does the P&L need YTD coverage?

acceptedAnswer.text: The statement must cover a full 12 or 24 months and be prepared or signed within 60 to 90 days of closing, depending on the program. A year-to-date statement alone does not satisfy a P&L-only program. Where the P&L is more than 90 days old at closing, the preparer re-issues it.

mainEntity.name: What credit score and down payment do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: P&L-only: 700 to 720 minimum credit across the programs I place, 80% maximum loan-to-value on a primary residence (20% down), 75% on a second home or investment property, and cash-out capped at 70% to 75%. Loan amounts cap at $1.5 million on most P&L-only options and up to $3 million on one. Reserves start at 6 months of the housing payment and step to 9 months above $1 million to $2 million and 12 months above $2 million to $2.5 million.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a P&L only loan as an S-corp owner?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. S-corp owners are a common P&L profile. The P&L can show the S-corp's results and the lender uses your ownership percentage to calculate qualifying income. If you take a modest W-2 from your S-corp and the rest as distributions, the P&L captures the full business income before owner compensation — usually qualifies you for far more than tax-return-based underwriting would.

mainEntity.name: What gotchas should I watch for?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three main ones. (1) P&L not matching deposits — if bank statements show way less revenue than the P&L claims, the file dies. (2) Implausible expense ratios — a consultant claiming 5% expenses or a contractor claiming 70% expenses will get flagged for review. (3) Preparer documentation — missing PTIN, missing letterhead, or wrong signature line. The P&L must look like a CPA prepared it, not a borrower typing into Excel.

mainEntity.name: How long do P&L only loans take to close?

acceptedAnswer.text: Typical close is 25–35 days. The bottleneck is usually getting the CPA or EA to issue the P&L on letterhead with the right signature block. If your preparer is responsive and you have the P&L ready at application, P&L only is among the faster Non-QM closes — less underwriter document review than bank statement, less back-and-forth than conventional.

mainEntity.name: Is P&L only available for investment property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but for most investment-property buyers a DSCR loan that qualifies on the rental income of the subject property is a cleaner fit. P&L only on investment caps LTV at 75–80% and usually prices similar to or higher than DSCR. For a primary residence or second home where personal income is the qualification path, P&L only is the right tool.

mainEntity.name: What about partnerships and multi-member LLCs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most P&L-only programs require at least 50% ownership; one accepts 25%. The P&L is for the whole business and your ownership percentage is applied to the net income. Below 50%, a K-1 analysis on conventional financing is usually the stronger path, and I model both.

mainEntity.name: What is a 1099-only mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Non-QM loan that qualifies you on one or two years of 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC income with a flat 10% expense factor, instead of tax returns or Schedule C. Gross 1099 income, less 10%, divided by the months in the period, is your qualifying income. You cannot own the company that pays you.

mainEntity.name: How is income calculated on a 1099-only loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Gross 1099 income times 0.90, divided by 12 or 24 months. $180,000 of 1099 income over 12 months qualifies at $13,500 a month. Two programs I place waive the 10% when the payer confirms in writing that you have no job-related expenses; one allows a lower documented ratio with a CPA certification. A 1099 issued to your business rather than to you needs a preparer’s expense letter.

mainEntity.name: Do I need 1 year or 2 years of 1099 history?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both options exist, and the one-year option is a documentation shortcut, not a history shortcut. It still requires two years with the same payer or in the same industry, tax transcripts, and year-to-date pay records or two to three months of bank deposits showing at least 90% of the prior year’s income. If you moved from W-2 to 1099 in the same line of work within the last 12 months, the one-year option is your route.

mainEntity.name: How is a 1099-only loan different from a bank statement loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 1099-only method starts with reported 1099 compensation; a bank-statement method starts with eligible deposits over the selected review period. Expense treatment and supporting records depend on the program. A contractor who receives 1099 income can still qualify using bank statements. Compare the supported calculations and full loan terms before choosing either method.

mainEntity.name: Can I combine multiple 1099 sources?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Lenders aggregate 1099s from multiple payers as long as they're in the same line of work. New sources started within the last 12 months are usually excluded from the average. A consultant with three steady clients all paying on 1099-NEC will see all three counted; a side gig that started six months ago typically will not.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: 660 minimum on the programs I place, at reduced leverage. 700-plus for the one-year option and better pricing; 720-plus for 90% loan-to-value on a primary purchase.

mainEntity.name: What about 1099-K from Stripe, PayPal, or Venmo?

acceptedAnswer.text: 1099-K is the messiest 1099 for mortgage purposes. The form reports gross payment processor flow, which can include returns, fees, and pass-through dollars that aren't actual income. Lenders treating 1099-K usually apply a higher expense factor (often 50%+) or require reconciliation to a P&L. If most of your income hits Stripe or PayPal, a bank statement or P&L loan is often a better fit.

mainEntity.name: I'm a real estate agent — does this work for me?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Real estate agents are one of the cleanest fits for 1099-only mortgages. Brokerages issue 1099-NEC, splits are predictable, and your gross commission income is well-documented. Some lenders pull MLS sales history to validate the 1099. Two-year averaging smooths out market cycles; a strong 12-month rebound from a slow prior year is a 1-year program candidate.

mainEntity.name: Will my Schedule C write-offs hurt me?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — that's the whole point. 1099-only programs do not pull tax transcripts and do not look at Schedule C. The qualifying income is your 1099 gross with a flat factor applied. If your Schedule C shows $80,000 net on $250,000 gross, conventional uses $80,000 and 1099-only uses $200,000–$225,000. The difference is often the entire loan approval.

mainEntity.name: Is 1099-only ever the wrong choice?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Three cases: (1) most of your income hits a personal bank account from cash or check side work, so bank statements are better. (2) Your true expenses are well above 10% and you need a CPA-prepared P&L to qualify accurately, so P&L only fits. (3) Your conventional qualifying income is actually higher because your write-offs are small, so a conventional loan wins and saves the rate premium.

mainEntity.name: How much down payment do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: 10% on a primary-residence purchase with 720-plus credit and two years of 1099 history, on the programs I place. 20% is the common entry point and opens the widest pricing. Cash-out caps at 80% loan-to-value. Loan amounts above $2 million require 20% or more and 6 to 12 months of reserves.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a 1099-only loan for a second home or investment property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes for second homes — LTV caps at 80% typically. For investment property, a DSCR loan that qualifies on the rental income of the property is usually a cleaner fit and prices better than 1099-only on a rental. We model both for your specific deal. Second-home 1099 deals work well for Texas borrowers buying Hill Country or coastal retreats.

mainEntity.name: Does the 1099 need to come from a US company?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes for standard programs — US-issued 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC. If you're a US tax resident contracting with foreign clients who don't issue 1099s, you'll need a bank statement program instead, since there's no 1099 to underwrite. For foreign nationals without US tax filings, that's a separate Non-QM product.

mainEntity.name: Is a 1099-only mortgage available in Austin, Travis County, and Williamson County?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — 1099-only programs are available throughout the Austin metro, including Round Rock , Cedar Park , Leander , Georgetown , Westlake , Bee Cave , Dripping Springs , Pflugerville , and surrounding counties. Pricing is competitive across the metro.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to live in Austin to qualify for a Texas 1099-only loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — the qualifying loan is for any Texas property, not tied to where you live now. I close 1099-only files for Austin metro buyers relocating from California, the Northeast, and other high-tax markets every month. What matters for underwriting is that your 1099 income is documented and consistent, and that the property securing the loan is in a state where I'm licensed.

mainEntity.name: What if I'm a 1099 contractor working for multiple Austin tech companies?

We combine the 1099s, apply the expense factor, and use the total qualifying income. Three to five payers is common in Austin tech consulting and underwrites cleanly.

mainEntity.name: What is a K-1 income mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A K-1 income mortgage is a conventional or jumbo mortgage where the borrower's qualifying income comes from a Schedule K-1 issued by a partnership (Form 1065) or S-corporation (Form 1120S). The lender uses Fannie Mae Form 1084 to convert tax-return income, add-backs, and distributions into qualifying cash flow. This is agency-eligible, not non-QM, when properly documented.

mainEntity.name: Why is the 25% ownership threshold important?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your ownership in the partnership or S-corp is 25% or more, Fannie treats you as self-employed. That triggers full Form 1084 cash flow analysis, business return review, and a current-ratio or quick-ratio liquidity test under Selling Guide B3-3.6-07. Under 25%, Selling Guide B3-3.4-19 applies instead: two years of signed personal tax returns plus the Schedule K-1, no business returns, and no viability analysis on the business. You still have to show the earnings were actually distributed to you or that the business can support withdrawing them — but the lender chooses how to document that. Note the boundary is 25% or more, so a borrower at exactly 25% is self-employed.

mainEntity.name: Can I use my K-1 distributions instead of ordinary business income?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lender uses your share of ordinary business income — not the distribution amount — as the starting point for qualifying income. Distributions are evidence the income is real and accessible, which the underwriter wants to see. Counting both would double-count the same money. The exception is guaranteed payments to partners, which are added separately.

mainEntity.name: What is the business liquidity test?

acceptedAnswer.text: When you own 25%+ of a partnership or S-corp, Fannie wants proof the business has enough current assets to support paying you the income you are using to qualify. The standard test is a current ratio of 1.0 or higher (current assets divided by current liabilities) or a quick ratio of 1.0 or higher for inventory-heavy businesses. Failed liquidity kills the income.

mainEntity.name: I'm a law firm partner — how does this apply?

acceptedAnswer.text: Law firm partners typically own less than 25% of the firm, which puts the file under Fannie Selling Guide B3-3.4-19. You document two years of personal returns and your Schedule K-1 — not the firm's 1065, which most partners have no authority to release anyway. W-2 wages from the firm document normally on top of that. The one thing that still gets tested is access to the earnings: either a distribution history consistent with the income being used, or evidence the firm can support the withdrawal. For equity partners at 25% or more, Form 1084 applies and the firm's books get reviewed. Guaranteed payments add on top with a two-year history.

mainEntity.name: What if my K-1 income is declining year over year?

acceptedAnswer.text: Declining income triggers heightened review. Fannie's general convention is that a year-over-year drop greater than roughly 5% requires the lender to use the lower of the two years and document a credible explanation. If the trend is sustained, the lower year is the qualifying number. A one-year anomaly can be explained around. Two years of decline is harder.

mainEntity.name: What add-backs are allowed on Form 1084?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common add-backs include depreciation, depletion, amortization, and non-recurring casualty losses, all taken at your ownership percentage. Business meals get a downward adjustment (50% of meals expense is added back since the IRS only allows half). Mortgages or notes payable in less than one year are subtracted as obligations. The full mechanics live in the form itself.

mainEntity.name: What if I'm a partner AND get W-2 wages from the same firm?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common for law firm partners and S-corp owners. Both income streams can be used. For S-corp owners, your W-2 from the company is part of your total cash flow analysis on Form 1084. For partnerships, W-2 wages are unusual (partners typically don't receive W-2s) but guaranteed payments serve the same function and add on top of ordinary K-1 income.

mainEntity.name: When should I go non-QM instead of agency on K-1 income?

acceptedAnswer.text: When the business fails the liquidity test, when depreciation buried the ordinary income, when the two-year trend is down more than 5%, or when the assets are strong and the returns are messy. The Non-QM programs I place qualify on 12 or 24 months of bank statements at a 50% default expense factor (lower with a qualified expense letter), on a CPA P&L at 700-plus credit and 80% loan-to-value, or on assets divided by 36 to 84 months. Ownership floors are higher than Fannie’s 25%: 50% for P&L and business-bank-statement methods at most investors, 25% for the personal-statement method. The rate premium is real; the loan amount usually is not available any other way.

mainEntity.name: How many years of K-1s do I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two years of personal returns with all K-1s, and two years of the business return at 25% or more ownership. One year is possible when the income is stable and the profile is strong. Where the second year is more than 5% lower than the first, the lower year is the qualifying figure and the drop needs a documented explanation.

mainEntity.name: What documents will you ask for?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two years of personal federal tax returns including all K-1s. Two years of the business return (Form 1065 for partnerships, Form 1120S for S-corps). Year-to-date business profit and loss. Current balance sheet for the business if 25%+ ownership. Government ID, asset statements, the appraisal, and the purchase contract. If under 25% ownership, the business return requirement often eases.

mainEntity.name: Can I use K-1 income to buy an investment property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — K-1 income qualifies for conventional jumbo, second home, and investment property loans the same way W-2 income does. For pure investment plays, a DSCR loan may be cleaner because it qualifies on the rental property's cash flow and skips personal income. We'll model both. See the investor loan guide for the comparison.

mainEntity.name: What is a bank statement loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bank statement loan uses eligible personal or business deposits as the primary evidence for a self-employed income calculation. The lender excludes non-income deposits, applies required expense and ownership treatment, and reviews the rest of the mortgage application. Deposits are not automatically qualifying income.

mainEntity.name: How many months of bank statements do you need?

acceptedAnswer.text: The selected program may use 12 or 24 consecutive months. Review income trends and seasonality, and confirm the acceptable account types. The statement period is separate from the minimum business-history requirement; neither a shorter period nor a longer one guarantees better terms.

mainEntity.name: Are bank statement loans legal, or are they a no-doc loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bank-statement programs still require verification of the income and other information used in the mortgage review. Covered consumer loans must meet the applicable repayment requirements. A statement-based calculation does not by itself establish compliance or determine qualified-mortgage status, and additional records may be required.

mainEntity.name: What credit score and down payment do you need in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single score or down-payment requirement for every bank-statement mortgage. The selected program, credit profile, property use, loan amount, and funds remaining after closing determine the available terms. Confirm the written requirements for the actual file.

mainEntity.name: Is a bank statement loan better than a conventional loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the income your records support and the complete terms. Review permitted tax-return adjustments before deciding a conventional loan will not work. Then compare current rates, fees, payments, cash needed, and reserves for the available options. More calculated income alone does not establish the better choice.

mainEntity.name: How do underwriters calculate self-employed income for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Underwriters start with the net income on your federal tax returns — not your gross revenue and not your bank deposits — then run a cash flow analysis using a worksheet like Fannie Mae Form 1084 or Freddie Mac Form 91. They add back paper deductions that didn't actually cost you cash, such as depreciation, depletion, amortization, casualty losses, and business use of home. Then they typically average the result over two years to get a qualifying monthly income.

mainEntity.name: What deductions get added back to self-employed income?

acceptedAnswer.text: For Schedule C filers, the standard add-backs are depreciation, depletion, amortization, casualty losses, and the business-use-of-home deduction. These are deductions that reduce taxable income but don't reduce the cash your business actually generated. What does NOT get added back: real cash expenses like vehicle costs, supplies, contract labor, meals, and travel. If you wrote it off and it was a real expense, it lowers your qualifying income.

mainEntity.name: Do I need two years of self-employment to get a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, but not always. Fannie Mae generally wants a two-year history of self-employment. There is an exception: with at least twelve full months of self-employment income on your most recent federal tax return, you may still qualify if you previously earned similar or greater income in the same field before going out on your own. Less than twelve months on a tax return is very difficult on conventional financing — that's usually a bank statement or non-QM conversation.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my self-employment income went down from one year to the next?

acceptedAnswer.text: Declining income changes the math. When income is stable or rising, underwriters average the two years. When the most recent year is lower, they generally can't use the higher average — the analysis leans on the lower, more recent figure, and the underwriter has to be satisfied the decline has stabilized. A one-time dip with a documented reason is workable. A steady downtrend is a harder conversation, and pretending it isn't there doesn't help you.

mainEntity.name: What if my tax returns don't show enough income to qualify?

acceptedAnswer.text: You have two real options. Option one is planning ahead: work with your CPA in the tax year before you buy so the returns show the income you actually earn — that trade costs some tax but buys qualifying power. Option two is a loan built for this exact situation: a bank statement loan qualifies you on business deposits instead of net tax income, and other non-QM programs qualify on assets or property cash flow. Aggressive write-offs don't end your homebuying plans — they just change which loan fits.

mainEntity.name: I just sold my company. How do I qualify for a mortgage with no W-2?

acceptedAnswer.text: On the sale proceeds, once they have seasoned 4 to 6 months in your account. The programs I place convert eligible assets to income by dividing by 36, 60 or 84 months, or test whether assets cover the loan balance plus 60 months of your other obligations. Cash counts at 100%, marketable securities at 80% to 90%. Business assets, restricted stock and funds still inside the sold entity do not count until they are in your name.

mainEntity.name: Can my RSUs count as income for a jumbo mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: They may, depending on the lender’s rules and your documented compensation history. Review vested and distributed awards, past receipt, the vesting schedule, and any employment or marketability restrictions. Restricted-stock income is also addressed in Fannie Mae’s conventional guidelines; it is not exclusively a Non-QM option. Shares already held as assets require a separate review, without double counting.

mainEntity.name: Can I buy a home in a revocable trust?

acceptedAnswer.text: Eligible revocable trusts can be accepted by conventional and other lenders. The lender and title company must review the trust, signing authority, property ownership, and the individuals qualifying for the mortgage. Holding title in a trust and using trust distributions as qualifying income are separate questions.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to move or pledge my brokerage assets?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not on the Non-QM asset programs I place: they verify balances, they do not take a lien or require a transfer. A bank’s relationship-pricing offer is a different product that may require moving accounts or pledging them as collateral. I put both on the table with the conditions spelled out, because a 25-basis-point discount tied to a $2 million transfer is not always the cheaper loan.

mainEntity.name: Will the lender need my brokerage statements and tax returns?

acceptedAnswer.text: Expect the lender to verify the accounts and income sources used for qualification. Required records vary by program and may include complete account statements, income documents, trust documents, or tax records. Start with a broad summary here; when documents are needed, I’ll arrange a secure way to share them.

mainEntity.name: Is a high-net-worth mortgage always a Non-QM loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A conforming loan up to $832,750 in the Austin-area counties, or an agency-eligible jumbo above it, fits when documented income supports the payment, and it will price better. Non-QM enters when the income is on the balance sheet instead of the tax return. I run both when the file allows it.

mainEntity.name: Can I use these approaches for a second home or investment property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Property use changes the available options and underwriting. Tell me whether you are buying a primary residence, second home, or rental. For an investment property, we can also compare rental-income approaches. A land purchase or construction project needs its own review; a home-purchase program does not automatically cover either.

mainEntity.name: Why not just use my private bank?

acceptedAnswer.text: A private bank can be a strong option, especially when relationship pricing fits your broader plans. Compare the rate and fees alongside required account transfers, pledged collateral, liquidity restrictions and ongoing relationship conditions. Asset-based mortgage qualification and a securities-backed loan are different products.

mainEntity.name: What's the rate difference versus a conventional or jumbo loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Asset-based loans usually cost more than a conventional or jumbo loan your documented income already supports. Lower loan-to-value files price better. For borrowers with the assets but not the W-2, the alternative is usually no loan at all, so I quote both whenever the file allows.

mainEntity.name: How does the 60- or 84-month divisor actually work?

acceptedAnswer.text: The program divides your eligible assets by a fixed number of months to create qualifying income. The programs I place use 36, 60 or 84 months; the shorter the divisor, the more income the same assets produce. Some programs use a coverage test instead: assets must equal the loan balance plus closing costs plus 60 months of your other obligations.

mainEntity.name: Can I include my retirement account if I'm under 59½?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, at a discount. Retirement accounts count at 70% before 59½, and at 80% to 90% once you’re past 59½ and can access the funds. Cash counts at 100% and marketable securities at 80% to 90%.

mainEntity.name: What's the minimum asset balance to qualify?

acceptedAnswer.text: There’s no single published minimum; the assets have to support the payment after the program’s divisor or coverage test. Plan for reserves too: often 6 months of the housing payment or more after closing, depending on the program and loan size.

mainEntity.name: Can asset depletion supplement my existing income?

mainEntity.name: How do conventional asset-based options compare?

mainEntity.name: What is a reverse mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reverse mortgage is a home loan that allows an eligible homeowner to borrow against home equity. Payments are generally deferred while program requirements are met, but interest and charges accrue and the loan balance generally grows.

mainEntity.name: Who may qualify for an FHA-insured HECM reverse mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: HECM borrowers are generally age 62 or older, use an eligible primary residence, complete required counseling, and must satisfy financial assessment and property requirements.

mainEntity.name: Does the homeowner still pay taxes and insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The homeowner remains responsible for property taxes, homeowners insurance, maintenance, and other applicable property charges. Failure to meet obligations can cause the loan to become due.

mainEntity.name: When does a reverse mortgage become due?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reverse mortgage generally becomes due after the last eligible borrower dies, sells the home, permanently moves out, or fails to meet loan obligations. Exact terms depend on the loan.

mainEntity.name: What alternatives should be compared?

acceptedAnswer.text: Depending on the goal, compare a traditional refinance, HELOC, home-equity loan, asset-depletion mortgage, retirement distributions, selling or downsizing, or using other assets.

mainEntity.name: I'm at 10 conventional loans — what now?

mainEntity.name: Can I cash out to buy the next investment property?

mainEntity.name: How do I finance a fix-and-flip?

mainEntity.name: What is BRRRR financing?

mainEntity.name: Do you do blanket loans across 5+ properties?

mainEntity.name: What's the best loan type for my first investment property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Compare conventional, DSCR, bank-statement, and asset-based paths based on income, rent, reserves, occupancy, and your plan. No program is automatically the best or cheapest choice for a first investment.

mainEntity.name: When does it make sense to switch from DSCR to a portfolio loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Compare the administrative benefits with the costs and cross-collateral risks when your portfolio changes. There is no fixed property count that makes a blanket loan better than individual loans.

mainEntity.name: Can I finance a 5-unit or 6-unit property?

acceptedAnswer.text: Properties with five or more units generally need a different financing review from one-to-four-unit residential properties. Available commercial or portfolio paths depend on the property, income, reserves, and lender.

mainEntity.name: Do investor loans show up on my personal credit report?

mainEntity.name: How many investment properties can I have financed at once?

acceptedAnswer.text: There’s no cap on DSCR loans. Fannie Mae limits you to 10 financed properties, so investors past that point usually move to DSCR or portfolio loans, which qualify each rental on its own rent.

mainEntity.name: Why are out-of-state investors buying so much Texas real estate in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three reasons. First, zero state income tax — California investors pay 9.3% on rental income; Texas investors pay 0%. Second, the population gain — Texas added more residents than any other state from 2020 through 2025 per U.S. Census data, and renters follow population. Third, corporate HQ migration: Tesla, Oracle, Charles Schwab, Caterpillar, Toyota, McKesson, HPE, Samsung have all relocated or expanded major operations to Texas in the last five years. Each of those moves brought thousands of W-2 jobs, which is rental demand.

mainEntity.name: Can I get a Texas DSCR loan if I live in California, New York, or anywhere out of state?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. DSCR loans are designed around the property, not your residence. You can live in California, Illinois, New Jersey, Washington, anywhere — and close on a Texas rental remotely. Mobile notary or e-closing handles the signing. You wire your down payment and reserves. The loan funds. Most of my out-of-state Texas DSCR closings happen without the buyer ever flying to Texas.

mainEntity.name: Will my California-based or out-of-state LLC work for a Texas DSCR loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most DSCR lenders prefer that the LLC holding title be either a Texas LLC or registered as a foreign LLC doing business in Texas. Foreign LLC registration with the Texas Secretary of State is $750. The cleanest path for most out-of-state buyers is to form a new Texas LLC for the property — formation is $300, and there is no Texas franchise tax for entities under approximately $1.23 million in annual revenue. A small number of DSCR lenders do allow direct vesting in an out-of-state LLC, but it limits your shop.

mainEntity.name: How does Texas property tax affect my DSCR ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: Texas property tax runs roughly 1.6 to 2.2 percent of assessed value depending on county and city — meaningfully higher than most other states. The trade-off is no state income tax. For DSCR underwriting, the lender uses actual property tax (or estimated tax based on purchase price) inside PITIA. On a $325,000 Texas single-family rental, expect $450 to $600 per month in property taxes alone. Out-of-state buyers used to California Prop 13 caps almost always underestimate this. Run your DSCR with the real Texas number.

mainEntity.name: What is the minimum down payment on a Texas DSCR loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard DSCR programs require 20 to 25 percent down for single-family and 2-4 unit properties. Strong-credit borrowers (740+) with DSCR above 1.25 can sometimes access 15 percent down options. No-ratio DSCR programs (which skip rental income calculation) require 30 to 35 percent down. Short-term rental properties — particularly in Hill Country — typically require 25 to 30 percent.

mainEntity.name: Are DSCR loan rates higher in Texas than other states?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. DSCR rates are priced on a national wholesale basis — Texas borrowers are not penalized for the state. mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a DSCR loan and a conventional investment property loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: The core difference is what the loan qualifies on. A conventional investment property loan qualifies on your personal income and debt-to-income ratio — you provide tax returns, W-2s or pay stubs, and the lender measures whether your income covers all your debt. A DSCR loan qualifies on the property's rent instead, using the Debt Service Coverage Ratio: monthly rent divided by the property's monthly principal, interest, taxes, and insurance. DSCR loans are made for a business purpose, so they sit outside the consumer ability-to-repay rule and don't require personal income verification. Conventional loans generally price lower; DSCR loans qualify more investors and close without touching your tax returns.

mainEntity.name: Is a DSCR loan or a conventional loan cheaper for a Texas rental?

acceptedAnswer.text: Conventional investment-property financing almost always carries a lower rate than a comparable DSCR loan, because it's a fully documented loan sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. A DSCR loan trades some rate for the convenience of qualifying on rent instead of personal income. The right question isn't which rate is lower in a vacuum — it's whether you can qualify conventionally at all, and what the lower-rate conventional loan costs you in tax returns, DTI room, and the cap on how many properties you can finance. For a W-2 investor buying their first or second rental, conventional usually wins on cost. For a self-employed or portfolio investor, DSCR often wins on access.

mainEntity.name: How many investment properties can I finance with conventional vs DSCR loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fannie Mae caps a borrower at 10 financed 1-4 unit properties when the new loan is for a second home or investment property, and reserve requirements increase as your property count rises. Once you hit that conventional ceiling — or once your debt-to-income ratio from existing mortgages blocks the next deal — DSCR loans have no such national cap, because they qualify each property on its own rent rather than stacking against your personal DTI. That's the practical reason most Texas investors who scale past a handful of doors end up on DSCR financing for the later purchases.

mainEntity.name: Do DSCR loans require tax returns in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A DSCR loan qualifies on the property's rent and your credit, reserves, and down payment — not your personal income — so there are no tax returns, W-2s, or pay stubs in the file. This is why DSCR is the standard answer for self-employed investors, 1099 earners, and anyone whose tax returns show strong write-offs that crush their qualifying income on a conventional loan. A conventional investment property loan, by contrast, requires the full personal income documentation package.

mainEntity.name: When should a Texas investor choose conventional over DSCR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choose conventional when you can document your income cleanly, your debt-to-income ratio has room, and you're still under the 10-property financed ceiling. Conventional financing rewards the W-2 or salaried investor with the lowest rate and the most favorable terms on the first several rentals. Move to DSCR when your tax returns don't support the income, your DTI is maxed out by existing mortgages, you're titling in an LLC, or you've hit the conventional property cap. Many investors I work with use both — conventional early, DSCR to keep scaling.

mainEntity.name: Can you get a DSCR loan if the property doesn't cover its payment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Standard DSCR loans want a ratio of 1.0 or higher, meaning the rent at least covers the full mortgage payment. But low-DSCR programs in Texas commonly go down to about 0.75, and no-ratio programs skip the calculation entirely. The lender accepts the shortfall in exchange for slightly different pricing, more equity, or stronger reserves depending on the program. Because DSCR loans are business-purpose loans secured by an investment property, the lender underwrites the property and the deal structure rather than your personal income, so a sub-1.0 ratio doesn't automatically kill the file the way a high DTI would on a conventional loan.

mainEntity.name: What is the lowest DSCR lenders will accept in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most standard DSCR programs set the floor at 1.0. Below that, lenders move into low-DSCR tiers — typically down to roughly 0.75 — where pricing can change, but the move from 1.0 into the mid-.70s is often manageable on a strong file. When the ratio falls below the lowest accepted band, the file moves to a no-ratio (or no-DSCR) program that ignores the property's income altogether and qualifies on the asset, the down payment, and reserves. Exact floors vary by lender and change with the market, so the real answer is the one your specific deal prices out to, not a published number.

mainEntity.name: What is a no-ratio DSCR loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A no-ratio loan is an investment-property loan where the lender does not calculate or require a debt service coverage ratio at all. Instead of proving the rent covers the payment, you qualify on credit, a larger down payment (often 25 to 35 percent), and cash reserves. It's used when a property cash-flows poorly on paper today — a value-add rehab, a short-term rental ramping up, or a second-home conversion — but the investor has the equity and reserves to carry it. You pay for that flexibility mostly through stricter LTV limits, reserve expectations, and pricing that depends heavily on the full file.

mainEntity.name: Do low-DSCR and no-ratio loans cost a lot more?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Low-DSCR pricing below 1.0 is usually a file-by-file adjustment, and the move down toward about 0.75 often is not dramatically worse when credit, down payment, reserves, and property story are strong. The bigger trade-off usually shows up when the file moves into true no-ratio territory or needs a lower LTV. The deal still has to make sense through appreciation, forced equity from a rehab, STR income, or rent growth — but sub-1.0 alone does not make it dead.

mainEntity.name: When does a sub-1.0 DSCR deal actually make sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: When the property is worth more to you than its current cash flow suggests. The four patterns I see work: a value-add rehab where you'll refinance into better terms once rents and value rise (a BRRRR bridge), a short-term rental whose projected income beats long-term market rent, an appreciation play in a supply-constrained Austin-area submarket, and a second home you plan to convert to a rental later. If the only reason for the sub-1.0 loan is that you overpaid or under-budgeted, better loan structure will not fix a weak deal.

mainEntity.name: Does Texas A6 apply to a DSCR cash-out refinance on a rental property?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Texas A6 (Article XVI, Section 50(a)(6) of the Texas Constitution) governs home equity loans secured by a homestead — a primary residence. Investment properties are not homesteads, so the 2% fee cap, 12-day waiting period, and one-per-12-months rule that apply to homestead cash-out refinances do not apply to a DSCR cash-out on a rental. That gives Texas investors meaningfully more flexibility on a refi than they have on their primary residence.

mainEntity.name: How much equity can I pull out with a DSCR cash-out refinance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most DSCR cash-out programs cap loan-to-value at 75% on a single-family rental. Some lenders go to 80% on strong-DSCR properties (1.25+) with excellent credit (740+). On a property appraised at $400,000 with a 75% cash-out LTV, the maximum loan amount is $300,000 — so if you currently owe $180,000, you'd net about $120,000 in cash, minus closing costs. Conventional investment-property cash-out caps at the same 75% on a 1-unit per the Fannie Mae Selling Guide, but DSCR doesn't require personal income to qualify.

mainEntity.name: How long do I have to own a rental before I can do a DSCR cash-out refinance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most DSCR cash-out programs require 3 to 6 months of seasoning from the original purchase date before you can use the appraised value rather than the purchase price. For a true BRRRR investor who bought with cash or hard money and rehabbed the property, this matters — you generally have to season at least 6 months before the lender will use the post-rehab appraised value to size the loan. A handful of lenders offer delayed-financing exceptions in the first 6 months but only up to the documented purchase price plus closing costs, not the new appraised value.

mainEntity.name: Can I do a DSCR cash-out refinance in an LLC?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. DSCR cash-out refinances can close in an LLC just like a DSCR purchase. If you bought the property in your personal name (because you used hard money or a conventional loan), you can refinance into your LLC at the same time as the cash-out. That gets the property into the entity structure where serious investors hold rentals and gives you the liability separation most CPAs and asset-protection attorneys recommend.

mainEntity.name: What's the typical prepayment penalty on a DSCR cash-out refinance?

acceptedAnswer.text: DSCR loans are non-QM products and typically include a prepayment penalty — most commonly a 3-2-1 or 5-4-3-2-1 step-down structure. On a 3-2-1, you'd pay 3% of the loan balance if you sell or refinance in year 1, 2% in year 2, 1% in year 3, then free and clear. On a $250,000 loan, that's $7,500 in year 1. Some programs offer a buydown of the prepay structure for a higher rate. If you plan to sell or refinance again within 24 months, model the prepay cost into the deal before you close.

mainEntity.name: Why is a DSCR cash-out better than a conventional cash-out for some investors?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three reasons: no personal income verification, no Fannie/Freddie 10-financed-property cap, and LLC title at closing. Conventional cash-out under the Fannie Mae Selling Guide requires full income documentation, counts against the 10-property financing limit, and can only close in an individual borrower's name. For self-employed investors whose tax returns understate income, for portfolio investors past property 6 or 7, or for anyone whose CPA structures rentals in LLCs, the DSCR path simply works where conventional doesn't.

mainEntity.name: Can I use Airbnb income to qualify for a DSCR loan in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — but only with certain DSCR lenders. Most non-QM lenders historically used a long-term-rent comp via Fannie Mae Form 1007 (Single-Family Comparable Rent Schedule) to qualify a rental, which produces a lower number than what a short-term rental actually grosses. A growing subset of DSCR programs now accept short-term rental income, typically using a 12-month AirDNA market projection with a vacancy and expense haircut. The lender you pick determines whether STR income is even on the table. I keep a running short list of which non-QM lenders currently accept STR income and at what haircut.

mainEntity.name: How is short-term rental income calculated on a DSCR loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: When STR income is allowed, most DSCR lenders use a 12-month gross revenue projection from AirDNA or a comparable market-data provider, then apply a 20–30% haircut for vacancy, cleaning, platform fees, and management before dividing by 12 to get a usable monthly figure. That monthly number goes into the DSCR formula as 'rent.' On a property AirDNA projects at $84,000/year with a 25% haircut, the monthly figure is $63,000 ÷ 12 = $5,250. If PITI is $4,200, DSCR is 1.25 — which qualifies on most STR-accepting programs.

mainEntity.name: Which Texas cities allow short-term rentals?

acceptedAnswer.text: STR regulation in Texas is local, not state-level, and rules vary significantly by city. Austin requires a short-term rental license under City Code Chapter 25-2 and has different rules for owner-occupied (Type 1) and non-owner-occupied (Type 2) properties, with Type 2 effectively capped in residential zones. Fredericksburg, Dripping Springs, and most Hill Country tourism markets allow STRs broadly but each has its own permit, occupancy tax, and inspection requirements. Before financing any STR, confirm the property's specific address is in a zone where short-term rental is allowed and that the existing license (if any) transfers to a new owner.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need for a DSCR STR loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most DSCR STR programs require 680+ credit, with the best rates available at 720+ and top-tier pricing at 740+. STR is treated as a higher-risk subset of DSCR — vacancy and revenue swings are real — so a few lenders require 700+ minimums on STR-income-qualified loans. Down payment is typically 20–25%, and 6–12 months of PITI in reserves is standard. If your scenario is right at a credit-score threshold, waiting 60 days for a score bump often produces a noticeably better rate.

mainEntity.name: Can I get a DSCR loan for a Hill Country Airbnb?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Fredericksburg, Dripping Springs, Wimberley, Marble Falls, and the broader Hill Country tourism corridor are active DSCR-STR markets. The 12-month gross revenue projection on a well-located Hill Country property often supports a strong DSCR even at 75% LTV, especially with peak summer and Wine Country seasons baked into the projection. Property type matters — purpose-built STR cabins or compounds often need a more specialized appraisal and may not fit standard SFR DSCR underwriting. Tell me the address up front; I'll confirm the property type underwriting before we go too far.

mainEntity.name: What's the down payment on a DSCR Airbnb loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: 20–25% down on most programs, same as a long-term-rental DSCR. 20% is possible at strong DSCR (1.25+) and 740+ credit; expect 25% as the floor on borderline DSCRs or 680–719 credit. Closing costs typically run 3–5% of the loan amount, plus 6–12 months of PITI in reserves required post-close. On a $600,000 STR purchase, plan for roughly $150,000 cash to close (down payment + costs + reserves) at 25% down.

acceptedAnswer.text: No. That's the whole point. A DSCR loan qualifies on the property's cash flow, not on your W-2s, tax returns, pay stubs, or debt-to-income ratio. original_complete_jsonld.description: A plain-English breakdown of what a non-QM loan actually is, why conventional underwriting rejects strong borrowers, and which non-QM paths exist for Texas buyers in 2026.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: What does non-QM mean on a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Non-QM means a loan doesn't meet the CFPB's Qualified Mortgage standard under 12 CFR 1026.43(e) — the rule that caps debt-to-income ratios and requires income to be verified using specific, standardized methods. It does not mean bad credit or high risk by default. It means the lender is documenting your income a different way, often because you're self-employed, an investor, or your money doesn't show up as a W-2. The lender still has to make a good-faith determination that you can repay the loan — that ability-to-repay requirement applies whether or not the loan is a QM.

mainEntity.name: Is a non-QM loan bad or risky?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not inherently. Non-QM is a documentation category, not a credit-quality label. I've closed non-QM loans for physicians, business owners with seven-figure net worth, and investors with dozens of properties — all denied by their bank not because they couldn't afford the home, but because their income doesn't fit a W-2 box. Pricing on non-QM loans tends to run higher than conventional because these loans carry more manual underwriting and typically aren't sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, not because the borrower is a worse credit risk.

mainEntity.name: Why did my bank say I don't qualify even though I make good money?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always it's how your income is calculated, not how much you actually make. Fannie Mae's underwriting guidelines require lenders to qualify self-employed borrowers off net income from tax returns — after every deduction and write-off — averaged over two years. A business owner who nets $40,000 on paper while running $250,000 through the business can look unqualified to a conventional underwriter even though the bank statements tell a completely different story.

mainEntity.name: What are the main types of non-QM loans in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: The core categories are bank statement loans (income based on deposits instead of tax returns), DSCR loans (investment properties qualified on the property's rental income instead of your personal debt-to-income), asset depletion loans (assets converted into a monthly income figure), 1099 and ITIN programs for non-traditional workers and non-citizen borrowers, and jumbo non-QM for high-net-worth buyers whose full financial picture doesn't fit standard boxes. Each has its own qualifying method — none of them are one-size-fits-all.

mainEntity.name: Do DSCR loans qualify off my personal income?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — that's the whole point of a DSCR loan. Conventional investment-property loans still qualify you off your personal debt-to-income ratio, with the rental income added in under Fannie Mae's rental-income guidelines. A DSCR loan flips that: the property's own rental income relative to its debt payment is what qualifies the loan, largely independent of your personal W-2 or tax-return income. That's why an investor with ten properties and complicated tax returns can often qualify for the eleventh through DSCR when a conventional loan would drown in the math.

mainEntity.name: What is the jumbo loan limit in Austin, Texas for 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: FHFA’s 2026 one-unit limit is $832,750 in Travis, Williamson, Hays, Bastrop and Caldwell counties; none is a high-cost county, so there is no high-balance step. That line is moving early: ahead of FHFA’s November announcement of the 2027 figure, several lenders have raised their internal conforming ceiling to $845,000 to $850,000, and I can place a loan between $832,750 and that ceiling on conforming pricing now instead of as a jumbo.

mainEntity.name: Is a jumbo loan harder to qualify for than a conforming loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not harder, but not standardized, and the numbers are wider apart than most articles admit. On the programs I place, minimum credit runs from 660 at 65% loan-to-value to 740 at the largest loan amounts; maximum loan-to-value runs from 90% on a sub-$2 million primary purchase to 55% at $5 million. Two lenders will give the same file different answers because they are reading different cells.

mainEntity.name: Do jumbo loans have to follow the ability-to-repay rule?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The ability-to-repay rule at 12 CFR 1026.43 applies to almost all closed-end consumer loans secured by a dwelling, and there is no loan-size exemption and no jumbo carve-out anywhere in its scope. Every jumbo lender must consider and verify eight underwriting factors, including income or assets, employment status, the mortgage payment, mortgage-related obligations, simultaneous loans, current debts, debt-to-income or residual income, and credit history. A jumbo loan may or may not also be a Qualified Mortgage, depending on the loan's pricing, product features, and points and fees — but ability-to-repay applies either way.

mainEntity.name: Can a self-employed borrower get a jumbo loan in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, four ways. Full documentation on two years of tax returns with a Fannie-style cash-flow analysis. Bank statements, 12 or 24 months, with a 50% default expense factor or a documented one. A CPA-prepared P&L, capped at 80% loan-to-value and $1.5 million to $3 million by program. Or assets, divided by 36 to 84 months. I have closed jumbo files on every one of them, and the documentation choice moves the cap more than the credit score does.

mainEntity.name: How much do I need in reserves for a jumbo loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: On the programs I place: 6 months of the full housing payment through $1 million to $2 million depending on the investor, 9 months to $2.5 million, 12 months to $3.5 million, and 18 months from $4 million to $5 million. Add 2 months per additional financed property at some investors, and 24 months on certain interest-only structures. Reserves are counted after your down payment and closing costs, and retirement accounts count at a discount.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: Should I Refinance in 2026? A Decision Guide for Austin Homeowners
original_complete_jsonld.description: A straight-answer refinance decision guide for Austin homeowners in 2026. Break-even math, rate thresholds, cash-out tradeoffs, and when waiting is the right call.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: When does it make sense to refinance a mortgage in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Refinance when your break-even point — the number of months it takes for monthly savings to cover the closing costs — is shorter than the time you'll stay in the home. The old rule of thumb was a 1% rate drop, but that rule ignores closing costs and how long you actually plan to keep the loan. In 2026, most Austin homeowners need to drop their rate by 0.5% to 0.75% and stay in the home for at least 3 years for a refinance to pay off. If you're planning to sell within 18 months, refinancing almost never makes sense.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate the break-even point on a refinance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide your total closing costs by your monthly payment savings. If closing costs are $6,000 and you save $200 per month, the break-even is 30 months — you need to keep the loan at least 30 months to recover the cost. If you plan to stay 5 years, a 30-month break-even is a good deal. If you might move in 2 years, it's a loss. The math is that simple. Don't let anyone sell you on a refinance without running this number first.

mainEntity.name: What are typical closing costs on a refinance in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Refinance closing costs in Texas typically run 2% to 4% of the loan amount. On a $400,000 loan, expect $8,000 to $16,000 in total costs, including lender fees, title insurance, appraisal, and recording. Texas has some unique rules — a cash-out refinance here is treated under Texas A6 law, which caps total fees at 2% of the loan amount and adds specific disclosure requirements. A rate-and-term refinance doesn't fall under A6 and has more standard pricing.

mainEntity.name: Should I do a cash-out refinance to pay off credit card debt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if you're confident you won't run the cards back up. Cash-out refinancing converts unsecured debt into debt secured by your home — that math works great on paper, but I've watched too many borrowers clear their cards, then fill them back up within 18 months and end up with both a bigger mortgage and the credit card debt again. If the underlying spending habit isn't fixed, the refi just gives the problem more runway. When it does work, it works well: replacing 22% credit card rates with a 7% mortgage rate can save thousands per year. Just be honest with yourself about the cause first.

mainEntity.name: How long does a refinance take in Austin in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: A standard rate-and-term refinance in Austin takes 25 to 40 days from application to funding. Cash-out refinances in Texas take slightly longer because of the mandatory 12-day waiting period between signing the A6 notice and closing. Appraisal turn times are the biggest variable right now — some Austin appraisers are out 10 to 14 days, others can get you in within a week. The whole process is faster than a purchase because there's no real estate contract, no inspection, and no seller to coordinate with.

mainEntity.name: Can I refinance if my home value dropped since I bought it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — you can usually refinance even if your home value is flat or slightly down, as long as you still have equity. Conventional refinances typically allow up to 97% loan-to-value on a primary residence rate-and-term, and FHA Streamline refinances don't require an appraisal at all in many cases. VA Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loans (IRRRLs) are similarly appraisal-light. If you're underwater — meaning you owe more than the home is worth — the options get narrower but aren't zero. Run the numbers with a lender before you assume you can't refi.
