original_complete_jsonld.headline: VA Loan Eligibility in Texas — Who Qualifies and How to Use Your Benefit
original_complete_jsonld.description: A complete guide to VA loan eligibility in Texas — service requirements, surviving spouse eligibility, Certificate of Eligibility, and how to use your VA benefit to buy a home.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: Who qualifies for a VA loan in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: VA loan eligibility in Texas is determined by your military service record. You generally qualify if you served 90 consecutive days of active duty during wartime, 181 days during peacetime, or 6 years in the National Guard or Reserves. Veterans who were discharged under conditions other than dishonorable are eligible. Surviving spouses of service members who died in the line of duty or from a service-connected disability may also qualify. Active duty service members are eligible after 90 days of continuous service.

mainEntity.name: Do National Guard members qualify for VA loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. National Guard and Reserve members who have completed 6 years of service qualify for VA loan benefits. Guard and Reserve members who were activated for federal service under Title 10 orders and served 90 days of active duty may qualify even sooner. Check your DD-214 or NGB Form 22 to confirm your service dates and discharge status, then apply for your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) through VA.gov or through your lender.

mainEntity.name: What is the VA loan limit in Texas for 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you have your full VA entitlement (meaning you've never used a VA loan, or you've paid off a prior VA loan and had the entitlement restored), there is no VA loan limit in Texas — you can borrow as much as a lender will approve with no down payment. The VA loan limit only applies to veterans with reduced or partial entitlement (for example, those who have an existing VA loan on another property). In those cases, the conforming loan limits set by FHFA apply to the entitlement calculation.

mainEntity.name: Can a surviving spouse use VA loan benefits?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. An unremarried surviving spouse of a veteran who died in the line of duty or from a service-connected disability is eligible to use the VA home loan benefit. Surviving spouses who remarried on or after age 57 and on or after December 16, 2003 may also be eligible. The surviving spouse applies for a Certificate of Eligibility using VA Form 26-1817 along with the veteran's discharge papers and the marriage certificate. A VA-approved lender can walk you through the documentation process.

mainEntity.name: Can you use a VA loan more than once?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the VA loan benefit is reusable. If you sell a home purchased with a VA loan and pay off the balance, your full entitlement is restored and you can use a VA loan again. If you still have an existing VA loan on a property, you can potentially use your remaining entitlement for a second VA loan — this is called a bonus or second-tier entitlement. Many veterans have used VA loans 2, 3, or even 4 times across multiple home purchases.

mainEntity.name: What is a Certificate of Eligibility (COE) and how do I get one?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Certificate of Eligibility (COE) is the VA document that confirms your eligibility for the VA loan benefit. Most lenders can pull your COE electronically through the VA's automated system in minutes — you typically don't need to request it separately. If you're working with a VA-approved lender, ask them to run it as part of your pre-approval. You can also request it yourself through VA.gov using your DD-214 for veterans, your NGB Form 22 for National Guard members, or your current statement of service if you're still on active duty.

mainEntity.name: How much equity do I need for a cash-out refinance in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: In Texas, you must retain at least 20% equity after the cash-out refinance. This is a state-level requirement under the Texas Constitution (Article XVI, Section 50). So if your home is worth $500,000, the maximum new loan amount would be $400,000. If you currently owe $250,000, you could potentially access up to $150,000 in cash.

mainEntity.name: What are cash-out refinance rates in Austin right now?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cash-out refinance rates in Austin typically run 0.125% to 0.50% higher than standard rate-and-term refinance rates. In March 2026, that puts most cash-out refis in the upper 6% to low 7% range for conventional loans, depending on credit score, LTV, and loan amount. As a broker with 40+ capital partners, I shop for the best rate on every file.

mainEntity.name: How long do I have to wait before doing a cash-out refinance?

acceptedAnswer.text: For conventional loans, most lenders require you to have owned the property for at least 6 months. For Texas cash-out refinances specifically, you must also wait at least 12 months from the closing date of any previous Texas Section 50(a)(6) loan before refinancing again. FHA cash-out refinances require 12 months of on-time payments.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a cash-out refinance to pay off debt in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Debt consolidation is one of the most common uses for cash-out refinances in Austin. Many homeowners use the proceeds to pay off high-interest credit cards, auto loans, or personal loans. The key is making sure the math works — trading 22% credit card debt for a 7% mortgage payment usually makes sense, but you need to factor in closing costs and your break-even timeline.

mainEntity.name: What are the closing costs on a cash-out refinance in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Closing costs on a cash-out refinance in Texas typically run 2% to 3% of the new loan amount. On a $400,000 loan, that's $8,000 to $12,000. This includes appraisal, title insurance, lender fees, and the Texas-specific attorney requirement for Section 50(a)(6) loans. Some of these costs can be rolled into the loan, so you don't always need cash at closing.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: How Long Does Mortgage Pre-Approval Take in Austin TX?
original_complete_jsonld.description: Mortgage pre-approval in Austin takes same-day to 3 business days depending on your situation. Here's exactly what to expect and how to speed it up.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: How long does mortgage pre-approval take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mortgage pre-approval typically takes same-day to 3 business days. If you submit your application and documents in the morning, most brokers can have a pre-approval letter ready by end of business the same day or the following morning. Complex files — self-employed income, multiple properties, recent credit events — may take 2–3 business days. Banks generally take longer than mortgage brokers for the same process.

mainEntity.name: What documents do I need for mortgage pre-approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a standard W-2 buyer: last 2 years of W-2s, last 30 days of pay stubs, last 2 months of bank statements, government-issued ID, and Social Security number for the credit pull. Self-employed buyers also need last 2 years of personal and business tax returns plus a year-to-date P&L. Having these documents ready before you apply is the single biggest way to speed up the process.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pre-qualification is a quick estimate based on self-reported income and debts — no credit pull, no document review. It takes minutes but carries little weight with sellers. Pre-approval is a full credit pull, income verification, and document review that results in a conditional commitment letter. In Austin's competitive market, sellers expect a pre-approval letter, not a pre-qualification. Pre-approval is what you need.

mainEntity.name: Does getting pre-approved hurt my credit score?

acceptedAnswer.text: A single mortgage credit inquiry typically reduces your score by 5 points or less — and only temporarily. Multiple mortgage inquiries within a 14–45 day window are treated as one inquiry by FICO, so shopping multiple lenders won't compound the impact. The credit score effect of a pre-approval is minor compared to the benefit of knowing your buying power and moving fast in a competitive market.

mainEntity.name: How long is a pre-approval letter valid?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most pre-approval letters are valid for 60–90 days. After that, the lender may need to re-pull credit and reverify income before extending the letter. If your financial situation hasn't changed, re-verification is quick — usually same-day. Don't let an expiring pre-approval slow you down if you're actively searching; just let your loan officer know and they'll refresh it.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pre-approved before I find a house?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — and you should. Getting pre-approved before you start your home search gives you a clear budget, makes your offers competitive from day one, and often reveals issues (income documentation, credit items) that are better addressed before you're under contract and on a deadline. In Austin, where homes can go under contract in days, having a pre-approval letter ready is not optional if you want to compete.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: FHA vs Conventional Loans Texas: When Each Wins
original_complete_jsonld.description: Below 640 credit: usually FHA. Above 680 with 5% down: usually conventional. The 3-question rule I use with Austin buyers, plus 2026 loan limits.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: What is the main difference between FHA and conventional loans?

acceptedAnswer.text: FHA loans are backed by the Federal Housing Administration and are designed for buyers with lower credit scores or smaller down payments — minimum 3.5% down with a 580+ credit score. Conventional loans are not government-backed and follow Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac guidelines — they require stronger credit but offer more flexibility on property type, mortgage insurance cancellation, and higher loan limits. The biggest practical difference is mortgage insurance: FHA requires it for the life of the loan (if you put less than 10% down), while conventional PMI cancels automatically when you reach 20% equity.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do you need for an FHA loan vs conventional?

acceptedAnswer.text: FHA loans accept credit scores as low as 580 with 3.5% down, or 500–579 with 10% down. Most conventional loans require a minimum 620 credit score, and the best rates don't kick in until 740+. If your score is between 580 and 639, FHA is usually your best option. From 640 and up, conventional often becomes competitive depending on your down payment and DTI.

mainEntity.name: Which loan requires less money down — FHA or conventional?

acceptedAnswer.text: FHA loans require 3.5% down with a 580+ credit score. Conventional loans can go as low as 3% down through Fannie Mae HomeReady or Freddie Mac Home Possible programs (for qualifying buyers), and 5% down as a standard option. The difference is small — but FHA's mortgage insurance is more expensive long-term, so a 5% conventional loan may cost less per month than a 3.5% FHA loan depending on your credit score.

mainEntity.name: Can you cancel mortgage insurance on an FHA loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you put less than 10% down on an FHA loan, the mortgage insurance premium (MIP) stays for the entire loan term — you cannot cancel it. The only way to remove it is to refinance into a conventional loan once you've built enough equity. If you put 10% or more down on an FHA loan, MIP cancels after 11 years. On conventional loans, private mortgage insurance (PMI) cancels automatically when your loan balance reaches 80% of the original home value — no refinance needed.

mainEntity.name: Is FHA or conventional better for first-time buyers in Austin?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your credit score and down payment. If your score is below 640 or your down payment is under 5%, FHA is usually the right starting point. If your score is 680+ and you can put down 5–10%, run both scenarios — conventional may cost less per month because PMI can be cancelled. In Austin's price range, FHA loan limits may also be a factor; the 2026 Travis County FHA limit is $571,550 vs. $832,750 conventional conforming, which matters when shopping above the FHA ceiling.

mainEntity.name: What are the FHA loan limits in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: For 2026, the FHA one-unit loan limit in Travis County is $571,550. The conventional conforming one-unit limit for Travis County is $832,750. If the home you're buying exceeds the FHA limit, you'll need a conventional conforming or jumbo loan. Limits are set by HUD (FHA) and FHFA (conventional) and update each January.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: 2026 Texas Down Payment Assistance Programs: TSAHC, TDHCA & City of Austin
original_complete_jsonld.description: Austin buyers can qualify for up to $40K in down payment help — even with income over $160K. TSAHC, TDHCA, City of Austin programs active now.

mainEntity.name: What down payment assistance programs are available in Texas in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: In 2026, the main Texas down payment assistance programs include the My First Texas Home program (up to 5% DPA as a 30-year deferred loan), the TSAHC Homes for Texas Heroes program (3–5% grant for eligible professionals), and the My Choice Texas Home program (open to repeat buyers). Travis County and City of Austin also run local DPA funds that periodically open for applications. Income limits and funding availability vary by program.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to be a first-time home buyer to get down payment assistance in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. The My Choice Texas Home program is specifically designed for repeat buyers. The Homes for Texas Heroes program is open to qualifying professionals (teachers, firefighters, law enforcement, veterans, nurses, and others) regardless of first-time buyer status. The My First Texas Home program does require first-time buyer status, defined as not having owned a primary residence in the past 3 years.

mainEntity.name: How much down payment assistance can I get in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Texas State Affordable Housing Corporation (TSAHC) offers 3% to 5% of the loan amount as down payment assistance, either as a grant (no repayment) or a second lien depending on the program. The TDHCA My First Texas Home program offers up to 5% as a deferred 30-year loan at 0% interest. On a $350,000 home, 5% DPA equals $17,500 — enough to cover most or all of your down payment on an FHA loan.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need for Texas down payment assistance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most Texas DPA programs require a minimum credit score of 620. Some programs will work with scores as low as 580 when paired with an FHA loan. The higher your credit score, the better your interest rate on the first mortgage — which matters because DPA programs attach to the first mortgage and the rate affects your monthly payment.

mainEntity.name: Can I use down payment assistance with an FHA loan in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Most Texas DPA programs are specifically designed to pair with FHA loans. FHA requires a minimum 3.5% down payment — DPA can cover that entirely, bringing your out-of-pocket to zero on the down payment. You still need to cover closing costs, though some programs can assist with those too. As a broker, I match each client to the DPA program that fits their loan type and situation.

mainEntity.name: Are Texas down payment assistance programs free money?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some are, some aren't. TSAHC grants are true grants — no repayment required. The TDHCA My First Texas Home second lien is a 0% interest deferred loan — you repay it when you sell or refinance, but there's no monthly payment and no interest accruing. Local programs like the City of Austin's DPA fund vary — some are forgivable after a set period (5–10 years), others are deferred loans. I go through the details on every program before recommending one.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: How to Buy Your Next Home Before Selling Your Current One (Austin, TX)
original_complete_jsonld.description: Buying a new home before your current one sells is a timing and debt-to-income problem with real solutions. How bridge financing, equity access, and home-sale contingency strategy actually work for Austin movers in 2026.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: Can I buy a new home before I sell my current one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The obstacle is almost never desire — it's two things: the equity for your down payment is tied up in the home you haven't sold, and the mortgage payment on your current home counts against your debt-to-income ratio when you qualify for the new one. Both have solutions. Fannie Mae will let a lender leave the current home's full housing payment out of your DTI if you provide an executed sales contract for it and confirmation that any financing contingencies have been cleared. If your current home isn't under contract yet, bridge financing or an equity-access strategy can cover the gap. The right path depends on your equity, your timing, and how much risk you want to carry.

mainEntity.name: How does my current mortgage affect qualifying for a new home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Until your current home sells, its full housing payment — principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and any HOA — counts in your debt-to-income ratio. Carrying two mortgage payments can push your DTI past program limits, which is why a lot of would-be move-up buyers think they're stuck. Fannie Mae's Selling Guide gives a path out: if your current residence is pending sale, the lender can exclude that payment from your DTI when you provide an executed sales contract and confirmation that financing contingencies have been cleared. No signed contract yet means the payment stays in your ratio unless another strategy covers it.

mainEntity.name: What is a bridge loan and when does it make sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bridge loan is short-term financing that lets you tap the equity in your current home to fund the down payment on your next one before the first home sells. The CFPB defines it as a temporary loan — typically 12 months or less — used to buy a new dwelling when you plan to sell the current one. It makes sense when you've identified the home you want, you have significant equity, and you need timing flexibility you don't have if you must sell first. It is not free money — it's a real loan with real costs, so it has to be weighed against the alternatives, not treated as the default.

mainEntity.name: Should I make an offer with a home-sale contingency?

acceptedAnswer.text: A home-sale contingency lets you back out if your current home doesn't sell — it protects you, but it weakens your offer, because the seller is now depending on a sale you don't control. In a competitive Austin market, a contingent offer often loses to a clean one. The strategy work is figuring out whether you actually need the contingency or whether bridge financing or an equity-access approach lets you make a stronger, non-contingent offer instead. Removing a contingency you don't need can be the difference between winning the house and watching it go to someone else.

mainEntity.name: Is buying before selling a good idea in the Austin market?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be the right move if you have significant equity, you're relocating or moving up and need to be in the next home on a specific timeline, and you want to avoid the cost and disruption of temporary housing and a double move. It's a worse idea if your equity is thin, your income can't comfortably carry both payments for a stretch, or the bridge costs outweigh the convenience. There's no universal answer — it's a math-and-risk decision, and the only honest way to make it is to run your actual numbers across every structure before you commit to one.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: Physician Mortgage Loans in Texas: How Doctors Qualify in 2026
original_complete_jsonld.description: How Texas doctors qualify with an employment contract instead of paystubs, how deferred student debt is handled, and when a physician loan beats conventional financing.

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: What is a physician mortgage loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A physician mortgage (or doctor loan) is a portfolio loan program built for doctors and dentists. It typically allows little to no down payment, waives private mortgage insurance, and lets a borrower qualify on a signed employment contract instead of paystubs. It also treats deferred or income-driven student loan payments more favorably than a standard conventional loan. It is fully underwritten under the same ability-to-repay standards as any other mortgage.

mainEntity.name: Can doctors get a mortgage before their job starts in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often yes. Fannie Mae's Selling Guide allows qualifying on a future employment offer when the start date is no earlier than 30 days before the note date and no later than 90 days after it, with a fully executed, non-contingent offer and additional reserves. Many Texas physician loan programs go further and let an attending or resident close on a contract that starts after move-in, which is why doctors relocating for a new position use them.

mainEntity.name: How do physician loans handle student loan debt?

acceptedAnswer.text: On a conventional loan, a deferred student loan is counted at the documented payment or 1% of the balance, and an income-driven payment can be used if it is documented and still in effect at closing. Many physician loan programs go further and use the actual income-driven repayment amount, or exclude deferred student debt entirely, which can swing your debt-to-income ratio enough to qualify when a conventional loan will not.

mainEntity.name: Do physician loans require PMI or a large down payment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Most physician programs allow 0–10% down with no private mortgage insurance, even above $1 million. Conventional financing with less than 20% down requires PMI. Removing PMI and the large down payment is the main reason a doctor early in their career chooses a physician loan over conventional.

mainEntity.name: Are physician loans only for MDs?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Most programs cover MD, DO, DDS, DMD, DPM, and often residents, fellows, and attendings. Some include nurse practitioners, physician assistants, veterinarians, and pharmacists. Eligible degrees and titles vary by lender, so the program has to be matched to your credential.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: ITIN Mortgage Loans in Texas: How to Buy a Home Without a Social Security Number
original_complete_jsonld.description: An ITIN by itself does not disqualify a borrower from mortgage financing. Fannie Mae accepts a valid Social Security number or an ITIN. What actually gates the file, which programs fit, and what Texas buyers need to document.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: Can you get a mortgage with an ITIN instead of a Social Security number?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The Fannie Mae Selling Guide states that each borrower must have a valid Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN), so the tax ID itself is not the disqualifier most borrowers assume it is. Fannie Mae also purchases loans made to lawful permanent and non-permanent residents under the same terms available to U.S. citizens. What matters is whether the lender can document lawful presence and whether the rest of the file — income, assets, credit — stands on its own. If it doesn't, portfolio ITIN programs outside agency guidelines are the fallback.

mainEntity.name: What is an ITIN and who is it for?

acceptedAnswer.text: An ITIN is a nine-digit tax processing number the IRS issues to people who are required to have a U.S. taxpayer identification number for federal tax purposes but who do not have and are not eligible to get a Social Security number. You apply with IRS Form W-7, along with documents proving identity and foreign status. The IRS is explicit about the limits: an ITIN does not authorize you to work legally in the U.S., does not qualify you for Social Security benefits, and does not provide or change immigration status. It is a tax number, nothing more.

mainEntity.name: Does an ITIN mortgage require a bigger down payment or higher rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends entirely on which lane the file lands in. If the borrower qualifies under agency guidelines, Fannie Mae's rule is that non-U.S. citizen borrowers get the same terms available to U.S. citizens — same down payment options, same pricing structure. If the file has to go to a portfolio ITIN program instead, expect a larger down payment and pricing above agency, because the lender is keeping that loan rather than selling it. Terms vary meaningfully from lender to lender, which is exactly why it's worth shopping the file rather than accepting the first quote.

mainEntity.name: What documents does an ITIN borrower need for a mortgage in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Plan on the ITIN assignment letter or evidence the number is current, government-issued photo identification, documentation of your status and lawful presence, and two years of filed federal tax returns showing the ITIN in use. Then the ordinary file: income documentation, two months of asset statements with sourced deposits, and a credit profile. If thin or no traditional credit is the issue, alternative credit — rent, utilities, insurance, phone — built over twelve months is often accepted, but it has to be documented from the start, not reconstructed under contract.

mainEntity.name: Can an expired ITIN hold up a mortgage closing?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can, and it's the most avoidable problem in these files. The IRS expires an ITIN that hasn't appeared on a U.S. federal tax return for three consecutive tax years — it lapses on December 31 after the third year of non-use. Renewal means filing another Form W-7 with original or certified identity documents, and that is not a turnaround you want to discover after you're under contract. Check the status of the number before you write an offer, not after.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: First-Time Buyer Assistance Programs Austin TX (2026): TSAHC, TDHCA & MCC
original_complete_jsonld.description: A complete guide to Texas first-time home buyer programs still available in 2026 — TSAHC grants, TDHCA down payment assistance, MCC tax credits, and how to stack programs to reduce out-of-pocket costs in Austin.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: What is the TSAHC first-time home buyer program in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: TSAHC (Texas State Affordable Housing Corporation) offers two programs for first-time buyers: the Home Sweet Texas Home Loan Program (open to all eligible buyers) and the Homes for Texas Heroes program (for teachers, firefighters, police, veterans, and other public servants). Both programs offer down payment assistance of 3–5% of the loan amount as either a grant (no repayment required) or a deferred second lien. You must work with a TSAHC-approved lender and meet income and purchase price limits.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to repay TSAHC down payment assistance?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on which option you choose. TSAHC offers two DPA structures: a grant option where the assistance is a true gift — no repayment ever — and a deferred second lien option where repayment is required when you sell, refinance, or pay off the first mortgage. The grant typically comes with a slightly higher interest rate on your first mortgage. Most buyers choose the grant because the simplicity is worth the rate difference, but run the math with your lender to see which structure is cheaper over your expected hold time.

mainEntity.name: Can I use TSAHC assistance with an FHA loan in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. TSAHC down payment assistance is compatible with FHA, VA, USDA, and conventional loans. FHA is the most common pairing because FHA allows a 3.5% down payment and the TSAHC grant can cover all or most of it. The combination means many buyers close with little to no money out of pocket for the down payment — though you'll still need to cover closing costs unless you negotiate seller concessions. Ask your lender to run both scenarios (FHA + TSAHC grant vs. conventional + TSAHC second lien) before deciding.

mainEntity.name: What is the Mortgage Credit Certificate (MCC) and how much can it save me?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Mortgage Credit Certificate is a federal tax credit — not a deduction — that lets first-time buyers claim up to 40% of their annual mortgage interest directly against their federal income tax liability, up to $2,000 per year. Unlike a deduction, a credit reduces your tax bill dollar for dollar. In Texas, MCCs are issued through TDHCA (Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs). A buyer paying $18,000 in mortgage interest in year one would get a $2,000 federal tax credit — every year for the life of the loan. Over 30 years that's up to $60,000 in tax savings.

mainEntity.name: Who qualifies as a first-time home buyer in Texas for these programs?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most Texas state programs, a first-time home buyer is defined as someone who has not owned a primary residence in the past three years. That means even if you owned a home before, you may qualify again after a three-year gap. Exceptions include buyers in federally designated target areas, where the first-time buyer requirement is waived entirely. Veterans are also often exempt from the first-time buyer requirement for certain programs. Income limits and purchase price caps apply and vary by county.

mainEntity.name: Can I combine multiple first-time buyer programs in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — stacking programs is one of the most powerful strategies available to first-time buyers in Texas. A common combination: TSAHC down payment assistance (grant) paired with an MCC tax credit through TDHCA. The DPA covers your down payment upfront; the MCC saves you money on federal taxes every year you live in the home. You can also combine these with seller concessions (seller pays closing costs) to get into a home with very little out of pocket. Not all programs can be combined — your lender will tell you exactly what's allowed based on your loan type.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: FHA Loan Requirements Texas 2026
original_complete_jsonld.description: Complete FHA loan requirements for Texas buyers in 2026: minimum credit score, down payment, loan limits, appraisal standards, and mortgage insurance explained.

mainEntity.name: What is the minimum credit score for an FHA loan in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: The FHA minimum is 580 for 3.5% down payment and 500–579 for 10% down. However, most lenders — including us — set their own overlay at 620 or higher. The FHA sets the floor, but lenders can add stricter requirements on top. If your score is between 580 and 620, you may qualify through FHA but will have fewer lender options. Below 580, you'd need 10% down and will find very limited lender availability.

mainEntity.name: How much down payment does an FHA loan require in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: FHA requires 3.5% down for borrowers with a 580+ credit score. For scores between 500 and 579, the requirement jumps to 10%. The 3.5% can come from your own savings, a gift from a family member, or a down payment assistance program — FHA is one of the most flexible loan types for sourcing funds. Texas has multiple DPA programs that layer on top of FHA: TSAHC and TDHCA both offer grants and second liens compatible with FHA.

mainEntity.name: What are the FHA loan limits for Texas in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: FHA loan limits vary by county and property type. For 2026, the limits for Travis and Williamson counties are $571,550 for one unit, $731,700 for two units, $884,450 for three units, and $1,099,150 for four units. Buyers should confirm the applicable county and property-type limit before relying on a figure.

mainEntity.name: Can you avoid FHA mortgage insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — FHA mortgage insurance is required regardless of down payment size. You pay two types: an upfront MIP of 1.75% of the loan amount (typically rolled into the loan), and an annual MIP that ranges from 0.45% to 0.85% of the loan balance, divided into monthly payments. For most borrowers putting 3.5% down on a 30-year loan, annual MIP is around 0.55%. Unlike conventional PMI, FHA MIP does not automatically cancel when you reach 20% equity if you put less than 10% down — it stays for the life of the loan. Many borrowers refinance out of FHA once they have equity and a stronger credit profile.

mainEntity.name: What does an FHA appraisal look for that a conventional appraisal doesn't?

acceptedAnswer.text: FHA appraisals check both market value and property condition. The appraiser is required to flag health and safety issues that a conventional appraiser might just note. Common FHA flags in Texas: peeling paint on homes built before 1978 (lead paint concern), missing handrails, roof with less than 2 years of life remaining, non-functioning HVAC, standing water or drainage issues, and exposed wiring. If the appraiser conditions the appraisal, the seller must make repairs before closing — or the buyer must use an FHA 203(k) rehab loan instead.

mainEntity.name: Can FHA be used for investment properties in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. FHA loans require owner-occupancy — you must intend to live in the property as your primary residence. You cannot use FHA to buy a straight rental property. The one exception is multi-unit properties (2–4 units): you can use FHA to buy a duplex, triplex, or fourplex if you live in one unit. That can be a strong strategy in Austin — the rental income from the other units can help qualify you and offset your mortgage payment.

original_complete_jsonld.description: Buying a condo in Austin TX? Here's what you need to know about warrantable vs. non-warrantable condos, HOA approvals, and how to get financing done right.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: What is a warrantable condo in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: A warrantable condo is one that meets Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines — which means it qualifies for conventional financing with standard rates. Requirements include: the HOA is not involved in any active litigation, no single entity owns more than 10% of units, at least 51% of units are owner-occupied, and the HOA maintains adequate reserves. Warrantable condos are the most financing-friendly option and usually have the widest range of loan programs available.

mainEntity.name: What is a non-warrantable condo?

acceptedAnswer.text: A non-warrantable condo fails one or more Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac requirements — it might have too many investor-owned units, active HOA litigation, inadequate reserves, or be a new construction project where less than 51% of units have sold. Non-warrantable condos can still be financed, but you need a portfolio lender or non-QM lender willing to hold the loan, and rates are typically higher.

mainEntity.name: What is a condo questionnaire and why does it matter?

acceptedAnswer.text: A condo questionnaire is a form the HOA completes that provides the lender with details about the building's financials, insurance, owner-occupancy ratio, pending litigation, and special assessments. Lenders require this on every condo purchase to determine whether the project is warrantable. If the HOA refuses to complete it, or if the answers reveal a disqualifying issue, it can kill the deal — even if the borrower is otherwise fully qualified.

mainEntity.name: Can you use an FHA loan to buy a condo in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but only in FHA-approved condo projects. FHA maintains a list of approved condo communities. If the specific condo development isn't on the HUD approved list, you cannot use FHA financing unless the project goes through FHA spot approval — a process that applies to a single unit in a non-approved building. Many Austin condo communities are not FHA-approved, so this is worth checking early in your search.

mainEntity.name: Are condo mortgage rates higher than single-family home rates in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Slightly, in most cases. Fannie Mae applies a loan-level price adjustment (LLPA) to condos that adds a small cost to the rate — typically 0.25% to 0.75% depending on your loan-to-value and credit score. For warrantable condos, this is a minor difference. For non-warrantable condos, the premium is larger. VA loans are an exception — condos financed with VA loans generally do not carry the same LLPA surcharges.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the HOA has a pending lawsuit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Any active litigation involving the HOA typically makes the condo non-warrantable for conventional financing. Minor litigation (a slip-and-fall claim covered by insurance, for example) is sometimes acceptable, but HOA lawsuits involving construction defects, neighbor disputes over common areas, or financial mismanagement usually disqualify the project. If litigation is active, you'll need a portfolio or non-QM lender who accepts non-warrantable projects.

mainEntity.name: How much do I need to put down to buy a condo in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a warrantable condo with conventional financing, the minimum down payment is 3% (with PMI) or 5% (without PMI for some lenders). VA loans allow 0% down for eligible veterans on VA-approved condos. FHA requires 3.5% on FHA-approved projects. For non-warrantable condos, most lenders require 10-25% down since these loans are held in portfolio rather than sold to Fannie or Freddie.

mainEntity.name: Can oil and gas royalty income qualify for a mortgage in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Royalty income can qualify, but conventional and government programs typically require heavy documentation — verifying the income source, the producing assets, and a multi-year continuance of the payments. Where that documentation burden is impractical, non-QM programs like asset depletion can qualify the borrower from verified assets instead of from the royalty stream itself. Program availability and guidelines change by investor, occupancy, and loan type.

mainEntity.name: What is an asset-depletion mortgage and who is it for?

acceptedAnswer.text: An asset-depletion mortgage qualifies a borrower by converting verified liquid and retirement assets into a monthly income equivalent for qualification, rather than relying on traditional employment or business income. It is most useful for borrowers whose wealth is clear on statements but whose income is unconventional, passive, irregular, or difficult to document — including retirees, royalty earners, trust beneficiaries, and high-asset borrowers.

mainEntity.name: Does a mortgage decline from a bank mean I won't qualify anywhere else?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A decline at a bank typically reflects that bank's product mix and overlays — most banks offer agency and jumbo products and few of the non-QM alternatives. A prior decline does not predict the outcome of a Non-QM review with a mortgage broker who can access bank statement, asset-depletion, DSCR, and P&L programs through the wholesale market. The fit between the file and the program matters more than the prior outcome.

mainEntity.name: How is asset depletion different from a bank statement loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bank statement loan qualifies income from a self-employed borrower's deposit history. Asset depletion qualifies from verified asset balances and works for borrowers who are not self-employed — retirees, royalty earners, trust beneficiaries, and high-asset/low-income individuals. The two programs solve different problems. The right one depends on whether the strongest part of the file is cash flow or net worth.

mainEntity.name: What is an asset depletion loan?

mainEntity.name: Can retirement accounts be used to qualify for a mortgage?

The payment calculator works forwards from a specific home price to tell you the monthly payment. Use affordability when you're house shopping. Use payment when you have a property in mind.

mainEntity.name: What is DSCR and how is it calculated?

acceptedAnswer.text: DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio) compares a rental property's gross monthly rent to its monthly PITIA payment (Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance, HOA). DSCR = Gross Monthly Rent ÷ PITIA. A ratio of 1.0 means the rent covers the payment exactly.

mainEntity.name: Is a DSCR below 1.0 automatically a bad deal?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Many investor properties in competitive Texas markets come in below 1.0 on a simple rent-to-payment calculation. That does not automatically mean weak pricing or a dead file. Credit, reserves, property type, rent source, loan structure, and program fit all matter.

mainEntity.name: Are DSCR loans available for primary residences?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. DSCR loans are business-purpose loans for investment properties only. They are not available for owner-occupied primary residences.

mainEntity.name: What is a temporary rate buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: A temporary rate buydown is a financing arrangement where the seller deposits a lump sum at closing that subsidizes the borrower's interest rate for the first 1–3 years. The loan is originated at the full note rate; the subsidy covers the payment difference each month.

mainEntity.name: Who pays for the buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Typically the seller or builder pays for the buydown as a seller concession. The funds go into a custodial escrow account and are released monthly to cover the payment difference between the reduced rate and the full note rate.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a 2/1 and a 3/2/1 buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 2/1 buydown reduces the rate by 2% in year 1 and 1% in year 2, then steps to the full note rate. A 3/2/1 reduces by 3% in year 1, 2% in year 2, 1% in year 3. The 3/2/1 provides more relief upfront but requires a larger seller deposit.

mainEntity.name: Does a buydown change my long-term interest rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A temporary buydown does not change your note rate, loan amount, or long-term amortization. After the buydown period ends you pay the full note rate. The loan always amortizes at the note rate; the subsidy only covers the payment difference during the reduced years.

mainEntity.name: What happens to leftover funds if I refinance or sell?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you refinance or sell before the buydown period ends, remaining escrow funds are typically applied as a principal reduction on your payoff. This makes buydowns attractive for buyers who plan to sell or refinance within a few years.

mainEntity.name: Is a seller concession the same as a buydown?

acceptedAnswer.text: A seller concession is any contribution the seller makes toward the buyer's closing costs. A buydown is one specific use of a concession. Conventional loans cap concessions at 2–9% of purchase price depending on LTV; VA and FHA have separate limits.

mainEntity.name: Is a wraparound mortgage legal in Texas?

acceptedAnswer.text: Owner/seller financing is legal in Texas and regulated under Chapter 5 of the Texas Property Code. WRAP mortgages require specific disclosures and must comply with SAFE Act requirements. Always work with a real estate attorney experienced in owner financing to structure the transaction correctly.

mainEntity.name: What is the 'due-on-sale' clause risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most conventional mortgages contain a due-on-sale clause that allows the lender to call the full loan balance due when the property is transferred. In a WRAP, the seller's existing mortgage stays in place without lender approval, which technically triggers this clause. The risk is real but lenders rarely exercise it when payments are current. An attorney can advise on structuring to minimize exposure.

mainEntity.name: What happens if the buyer stops paying?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the buyer defaults on the WRAP loan, you must continue paying your underlying mortgage to protect your credit and avoid foreclosure on your existing lien. You can then foreclose on the buyer through the owner-finance process. This is why proper legal documentation and a solid down payment are critical.

mainEntity.name: How is the WRAP interest rate set?

acceptedAnswer.text: You and the buyer negotiate the WRAP rate. It should be high enough to generate meaningful spread above your existing rate, but low enough to attract buyers who can't or won't take a conventional loan at current market rates. Rates typically range from 1-3% above your existing rate, and below current market rates for the buyer.

mainEntity.name: Does the buyer know about my existing mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — ethical and legal seller financing requires full disclosure. The buyer must understand the WRAP structure, including your existing loan balance, rate, and the due-on-sale risk. Texas Property Code requires specific disclosures in owner-finance transactions.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to buy a house in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: From the day you go under contract to closing, the timeline depends on program, property, appraisal, title, and documentation in Austin TX. The full process — from deciding to buy to closing — is usually 60–90 days when you factor in pre-approval, home search, and contract-to-close time. Getting pre-approved before you start searching is the single most important step to compress the timeline.

mainEntity.name: How much money do I need to buy a house in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: You need your down payment plus closing costs. Down payment ranges from 0% (VA and USDA loans) to 3–5% (FHA and conventional programs for first-time buyers) to 20% (conventional, to avoid PMI). Closing costs in Austin typically run 2–3% of the purchase price. On a $450,000 home with 5% down, plan for roughly $22,500 down and $9,000–$13,500 in closing costs, though seller concessions or lender credits can offset much of the closing cost side.

mainEntity.name: What is the option period in Texas and how does it work?

acceptedAnswer.text: The option period is a Texas-specific due diligence window — typically 7–10 days — during which you pay a small option fee (usually $100–$500) to the seller for the right to terminate the contract for any reason and get your earnest money back. During this window, you complete the home inspection, negotiate any repairs or price adjustments, and finalize your financing. If you walk away before the option period ends, you forfeit only the option fee, not your full earnest money deposit.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a real estate agent to buy a house in Austin?

acceptedAnswer.text: You're not legally required to use an agent, but it's highly recommended in Austin's competitive market. A buyer's agent represents your interests, helps you write competitive offers, negotiates on your behalf, and coordinates inspections and the option period — at no cost to you (the seller traditionally pays buyer agent commission, though this is evolving post-2024 NAR settlement). In a market where multiple-offer situations are common, an experienced buyer's agent is a meaningful competitive advantage.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need to buy a house in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Minimum credit scores by loan type: FHA requires 580 with 3.5% down (or 500 with 10% down); conventional requires 620 minimum (though 740+ gets the best rates); VA has no official minimum but most lenders set 580–620; USDA typically requires 640. A higher credit score directly reduces your interest rate — the difference between a 680 and 760 score on a $400,000 conventional loan can be 0.5% in rate, which is roughly $130/month.

mainEntity.name: What are closing costs in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Closing costs in Austin TX typically run 2–3% of the purchase price for buyers. They include lender fees (origination, underwriting), title insurance and escrow fees, prepaid items (homeowner's insurance, property tax escrow, prepaid interest), and appraisal. On a $450,000 home, expect $9,000–$13,500. You can negotiate seller concessions to offset closing costs, especially in slower markets. Lender credits (accepting a slightly higher rate in exchange for cash toward closing costs) are another option.

mainEntity.name: How long does mortgage pre-approval take in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: With all documents ready, mortgage pre-approval typically takes one to two business days. In urgent situations, same-day pre-approvals are possible. The timeline depends primarily on how quickly you can provide the required documentation — income, assets, identification, and tax returns. Working with a mortgage broker rather than a big bank typically means faster turnaround because decisions aren't stuck in a centralized processing queue.

mainEntity.name: What documents do I need for mortgage pre-approval in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard documents include: last 2 pay stubs, 2 years of W-2s, 2 years of federal tax returns (all pages and schedules), 2 months of bank statements (all pages, all accounts), a government-issued photo ID, and your Social Security number. Self-employed borrowers also need business tax returns and a year-to-date profit and loss statement. VA loan applicants need their Certificate of Eligibility or DD-214.

mainEntity.name: Does mortgage pre-approval expire?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Most pre-approval letters are valid for 60–90 days. After that, updated income and asset documentation may be required to re-verify your financial situation. Your credit inquiry is valid for 120 days, so a new credit pull is not always necessary for a renewal. If you're not actively house hunting, it's still worth getting pre-approved early to identify any issues you can address before searching.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pre-qualification is a quick estimate based on self-reported, unverified information — no documents verified, no credit pull. Pre-approval involves a full review of your financial documents and a hard credit inquiry. In Austin's competitive market, sellers and listing agents expect to see a pre-approval letter — not a pre-qualification — before accepting an offer. A pre-qualification letter won't win a bidding war. A lender-reviewed pre-approval will.

mainEntity.name: Does getting pre-approved for a mortgage hurt my credit score?

acceptedAnswer.text: A pre-approval requires a hard credit inquiry, which typically lowers your score by 2–5 points temporarily. The impact is minor and usually recovers within 1–2 months. Multiple mortgage inquiries within a 14–45 day window are treated as a single inquiry by FICO, so shopping multiple lenders during that window won't compound the damage.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pre-approved if I'm self-employed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — self-employed borrowers can absolutely get pre-approved. You'll need 2 years of personal and business tax returns, a year-to-date profit and loss statement, and 2 months of business bank statements. The key difference is that lenders use your net income (after deductions) from tax returns, not gross revenue. If your returns show heavy write-offs, some non-QM loan programs qualify on bank statement income instead.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need to get pre-approved in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: Credit score requirements depend on the loan type. FHA loans allow scores as low as 580 (with 3.5% down) or 500–579 (with 10% down). Conventional loans typically require 620+. VA loans technically have no minimum score set by the VA, but most lenders want 580–620+. The higher your score, the better your rate. Scores of 740+ get the best conventional pricing.

mainEntity.name: What happens after I get pre-approved — what are the next steps?

acceptedAnswer.text: After pre-approval, you work with your real estate agent to find a home and make an offer. Once your offer is accepted, you'll formally apply for the loan with the specific property address. The lender orders an appraisal, processes your file through underwriting, and clears any conditions. Once all conditions are met, you receive a Clear to Close. You sign your final documents at the title company and receive your keys. The time from contract to close is typically 21–35 days.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a fixed-rate and adjustable-rate mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A fixed-rate mortgage has an interest rate that never changes, so your monthly payment stays the same for the life of the loan. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) starts with a lower fixed rate for an initial period — typically 5, 7, or 10 years — then adjusts annually based on a market index.

mainEntity.name: When does an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) make sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: An ARM can make sense if you plan to sell or refinance within the initial fixed period, or if you expect interest rates to drop significantly. ARMs typically offer lower starting rates than 30-year fixed loans, which can mean meaningful savings during the initial period.

mainEntity.name: Is a fixed-rate mortgage better for buying a home in Austin TX?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most Austin buyers planning to stay 7+ years, a fixed-rate mortgage offers predictability and long-term payment stability. If rates drop after you buy, you can always refinance into a lower fixed rate without the uncertainty of annual ARM adjustments.

mainEntity.name: What is a 5/1 ARM mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 5/1 ARM has a fixed interest rate for the first 5 years, then adjusts once per year after that based on a benchmark index (like SOFR) plus a margin set by the lender. The '5' refers to the initial fixed period in years, and the '1' indicates it adjusts annually after that.

mainEntity.name: How much lower is the rate on an ARM compared to a 30-year fixed mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Historically, 5/1 ARM starting rates run 0.5-1.0% below 30-year fixed rates. However, the spread varies based on current market conditions. When the yield curve is flat or inverted — as it has been in recent years — the advantage of an ARM can narrow significantly.

mainEntity.name: What credit score do I need to qualify for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Minimum scores vary by loan type: 620 for conventional loans, 580 for FHA with 3.5% down (or 500 with 10% down), and 620 for VA loans. A higher score unlocks better rates — even a 20-point improvement can save thousands in interest over the life of the loan.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to improve my credit score enough to get a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Paying down credit card balances can improve your score within 30-60 days. Disputing errors on your credit report can also show quick improvement. More serious issues like collections, charge-offs, or late payments typically take 6-24 months to recover from, depending on severity.

mainEntity.name: Does getting a mortgage pre-approval hurt my credit score?

acceptedAnswer.text: A pre-approval requires a hard credit inquiry, which typically lowers your score by 2-5 points temporarily. Multiple mortgage inquiries within a 14-45 day window are treated as a single inquiry by the credit bureaus, so shopping multiple lenders during that period won't cause additional damage.

mainEntity.name: What factors affect my credit score most for mortgage approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: Payment history is the biggest factor at 35% of your score — every on-time payment helps, every late payment hurts. Credit utilization (how much of your available credit you're using) accounts for 30%. Length of credit history is 15%, while new credit accounts and credit mix each contribute 10%.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay off collections before applying for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the loan type and the collection balance. Some loan programs allow collections to remain unpaid if they are older or below a certain threshold. However, paying or settling collections can improve your score — and removing them via a pay-for-delete agreement is even better. Consult your loan officer before paying off old collections, as it can sometimes trigger a temporary score drop.

mainEntity.name: What is DTI in a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: DTI (Debt-to-Income ratio) is the percentage of your gross monthly income that goes toward monthly debt payments. Lenders use two DTI numbers: front-end DTI (housing payment only) and back-end DTI (all debts including housing, car loans, student loans, and credit cards). Most conventional loans require a back-end DTI below 45%, though some programs allow up to 50%. A lower DTI means you qualify for more loan programs and better rates.

mainEntity.name: What is LTV in a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: LTV (Loan-to-Value ratio) is the percentage of the home's value covered by your mortgage. If you buy a $400,000 home with $80,000 down (20%), your LTV is 80%. LTV determines whether you need PMI, what rate you qualify for, and which loan programs are available. Lower LTV means less risk for the lender and typically a lower rate for the borrower.

mainEntity.name: What is PMI and when do I have to pay it?

acceptedAnswer.text: PMI (Private Mortgage Insurance) is required on conventional loans when your down payment is less than 20% — meaning your LTV is above 80%. PMI protects the lender (not you) if you default. PMI rates typically run 0.3%–1.5% of the loan amount per year. PMI automatically cancels when your LTV reaches 78% of the original purchase price. You can also request removal when you reach 80% LTV based on current market value by paying for a new appraisal.

mainEntity.name: What is a mortgage rate lock?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rate lock is a lender's guarantee to hold a specific interest rate and points for a defined period — typically 15 to 60 days — while your loan processes. If rates rise before closing, your locked rate stays the same. If rates fall, your locked rate stays the same (unless you negotiate a float-down option). Lock periods expire: missing your closing date means re-locking, often at a higher cost.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pre-qualification is an informal estimate of what you might borrow based on self-reported income and assets — no credit check, no document review. Pre-approval is a formal lender review: your credit is pulled, income and assets are verified, and the lender issues a written commitment for a specific loan amount. In Austin's competitive market, sellers typically require a pre-approval letter, not just a pre-qualification, before accepting an offer.

mainEntity.name: What does Clear to Close (CTC) mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clear to Close (CTC) means the underwriter has reviewed and approved all loan conditions — your file is fully approved and ready to fund. After CTC, you'll receive your final Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing (required by TRID). CTC is the finish line of the mortgage process before you sign and get your keys.

mainEntity.name: Is a lower APR always better?

If you sell or refinance in 5–7 years — which most people do — a loan with higher APR but lower upfront fees can cost less overall. acceptedAnswer.text: Not automatically. APR is one data point, not the whole picture. If two loans have identical terms and you plan to keep the loan for 20+ years, the lower APR is usually the better deal. But if you expect to move or refinance within 5–10 years, calculate total cost over your actual holding period instead. Take (monthly payment times number of months) plus total closing costs for each option. That gives you a real apples-to-apples comparison.

acceptedAnswer.text: A correspondent lender funds loans in its own name using its own warehouse line of credit, then sells the closed loan to investors. That's different from a broker, who submits files to a wholesale lender that funds in their name. For borrowers, the correspondent model usually means faster closings, more control over conditions and pricing, and competitive wholesale-style rates without the retail markup of a big bank or online lender. Adam Styer is a correspondent lender licensed in Texas and can also broker deals when wholesale pricing makes more sense for the specific loan.

mainEntity.name: Will switching lenders delay my closing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. If you switch early — within the first week after going under contract — most closings stay on schedule. The biggest delay risk is the appraisal. If it can't transfer to the new lender, ordering a new one adds 5 to 10 business days. The switch itself (new application, document submission) only takes a day.

mainEntity.name: Can I transfer my appraisal to a new lender?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the loan type and how the appraisal was ordered. FHA and VA appraisals are tied to the property, not the lender, so they transfer automatically. Conventional appraisals ordered through a standard appraisal management company (AMC) can sometimes transfer if the new lender uses the same AMC. Appraisals ordered through a lender's internal panel typically cannot transfer and you will need a new one.

mainEntity.name: How late in the process can I switch mortgage lenders?

acceptedAnswer.text: As a rule of thumb, if you have 21 or more days to closing, switching is straightforward. With 14 to 21 days, it's doable but tight — call the new lender first and ask if they can meet the timeline. With less than 14 days, it becomes risky and depends on factors like appraisal transferability and file complexity. An experienced broker can give you an honest answer before you commit.

mainEntity.name: What should I compare besides the interest rate on a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Beyond the interest rate, compare origination charges (Section A on the Loan Estimate), discount points versus lender credits, the rate lock period and extension fees, estimated closing timeline, and whether the lender requires escrow reserves. These six factors can swing your total loan cost by thousands of dollars — even when two lenders quote the exact same rate.

mainEntity.name: What are origination charges on a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Origination charges are the fees a lender charges to process and underwrite your loan. They appear in Section A of page 2 on your Loan Estimate. These charges vary widely between lenders — one might charge $1,000 while another charges $5,000 for the same rate. This is the single biggest variable in total loan cost that most borrowers overlook when comparing offers.

mainEntity.name: How do discount points affect my mortgage cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Discount points are upfront fees you pay to buy a lower interest rate. One point equals 1% of the loan amount. Paying points lowers your monthly payment but increases your cash to close. Whether points save you money depends on how long you keep the loan — if you sell or refinance before you recoup the upfront cost through lower payments, points cost you more than they save.

mainEntity.name: Should I wait for mortgage rates to drop before buying a home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Waiting for rates to drop usually costs more than it saves. Every month you wait, you pay rent instead of building equity. When rates do drop, buyer demand surges and home prices rise — often offsetting the rate savings entirely. The better question is whether you're financially ready to buy today.

mainEntity.name: What happens to home prices when mortgage rates drop?

acceptedAnswer.text: When rates drop, purchasing power increases across the buyer pool, which drives up demand and typically pushes home prices higher — sometimes quickly. Buyers who waited for the rate drop end up competing against more buyers for the same homes, often at higher prices. The rate savings can be partially or fully erased by a higher purchase price.

mainEntity.name: Can I refinance my mortgage later if rates drop after I buy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. This is the 'marry the house, date the rate' strategy. You buy now at current rates and refinance when rates improve. Refinancing typically costs 1-3% of the loan amount and breaks even within 18-36 months. You get to lock in today's home price while still benefiting from future rate drops.

mainEntity.name: How do Austin TX buyers decide when to buy a home?

acceptedAnswer.text: The best time to buy depends more on personal readiness than on market conditions. If you have stable income, adequate savings for down payment and reserves, a solid credit profile, and plan to stay at least 3-5 years, the math typically favors buying sooner rather than waiting for perfect rates.

mainEntity.name: What is the 'date the rate, marry the house' strategy?

acceptedAnswer.text: This means focusing on finding the right home at today's price, accepting current interest rates, and planning to refinance when rates eventually fall. The strategy eliminates the risk of being priced out of the market while waiting for rate improvement — and lets you start building equity immediately.

mainEntity.name: Why might an advisor evaluate a reverse mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: An advisor may evaluate a reverse mortgage when home equity could support retirement cash flow, reduce sequence-of-returns pressure, fund housing needs, or preserve other liquidity, subject to costs and obligations.

mainEntity.name: Does a reverse mortgage eliminate homeowner expenses?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Property taxes, insurance, maintenance, occupancy, and applicable property charges remain the homeowner’s responsibility.

mainEntity.name: How does a reverse mortgage affect heirs?

acceptedAnswer.text: The balance generally grows and reduces remaining equity. When due, heirs may have options to repay the debt and retain the home, sell it, or follow the applicable servicer process.

mainEntity.name: Should asset depletion be considered first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Asset depletion should be included in the comparison when eligible assets could support a forward mortgage. The right order depends on the client’s cash-flow, liquidity, estate, and housing objectives.

original_complete_jsonld.description: When a buyer gets declined, the deal usually isn't dead. The loan options that exist for self-employed, investor, and high-net-worth clients who don't fit conventional guidelines.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: My buyer was just declined — is it worth sending the file to another loan officer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always. A mortgage decline is usually a guideline mismatch, not a verdict on the buyer. Send the scenario, the income, and the reason for the denial, and you can typically find out within about a day whether there is a path forward through a non-conventional program.

mainEntity.name: What kinds of buyers usually don't fit conventional mortgage financing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Self-employed business owners whose tax returns show little income, real estate investors who have hit the conventional property limit, buyers paid largely in bonuses, stock, or partnership distributions, and high-net-worth clients who are asset-rich but do not show traditional income.

mainEntity.name: What loan programs work for buyers who don't fit conventional guidelines?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the file. A bank statement loan qualifies on deposits instead of tax returns, asset depletion qualifies on liquid assets, and a portfolio investor loan qualifies on the property's rental income with no limit on the number of properties owned. These are non-QM portfolio products designed for profiles outside conventional underwriting.

mainEntity.name: How fast can a loan officer tell me whether there's a path for a declined buyer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually the same day — a quick yes or no either way, so the agent and buyer can move forward with confidence.

original_complete_jsonld.headline: When Strong Buyers Don't Fit Conventional: 6 Scenarios and the Loans That Solve Them
original_complete_jsonld.description: Strong buyers get stuck when conventional guidelines weren't built for how they manage money. Six common scenarios and how we structure around each one.

worksFor.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

publisher.name: Kyber Mortgage Corporation dba HyperSmart Home Loans

mainEntity.name: What does it mean when a buyer doesn't fit conventional financing?

acceptedAnswer.text: It means the buyer's finances don't match the documentation conventional guidelines expect — usually a W-2, two years of tax returns showing steady income, and enough liquid cash on hand. Successful people often hold their money differently: equity tied up in a current home, income offset by business write-offs, wealth held in assets rather than salary, or cash flow that shows up in deposits but not on a tax return. Not fitting the conventional box is a documentation mismatch, not a verdict on whether the buyer qualifies.

mainEntity.name: Can a buyer purchase a new home before selling their current one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The obstacle is debt-to-income — carrying both mortgage payments usually pushes the buyer over the limit. Buy-before-you-sell programs and bridge financing solve this by letting the buyer access the equity in their current home for the down payment, make a non-contingent offer, and move once, instead of selling first and scrambling to find the next home.

mainEntity.name: How does a real estate investor qualify without enough personal income?

acceptedAnswer.text: With a DSCR loan. DSCR (debt-service-coverage-ratio) loans qualify on the rental income the property itself produces rather than the borrower's personal tax returns or debt-to-income ratio. If the property's rent covers its payment, the deal works — which is why investors who already own several properties can keep buying.

mainEntity.name: How can an asset-rich but low-income buyer qualify for a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Through asset depletion. This structure converts a buyer's eligible liquid assets — savings, brokerage accounts, retirement funds — into a qualifying monthly income figure, so a retiree or asset-heavy buyer with little W-2 income can still document the ability to repay.

mainEntity.name: How do self-employed buyers qualify when their tax returns understate their income?

acceptedAnswer.text: With a bank statement loan. Instead of Schedule C net income after write-offs, the lender uses 12 to 24 months of business or personal bank deposits to establish qualifying income. It reflects what the business actually earns, which is often far more than the tax return shows.

mainEntity.name: Does using a non-conventional loan mean a worse deal for the buyer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily, and often it's the difference between closing and not closing at all. These are portfolio and non-QM programs built for specific profiles. The right move is to structure the loan correctly from the start rather than force a strong buyer into a box they were never going to fit — a ten-minute conversation before the offer is written usually saves a lot of pain later.
